But the most terrible thing is:
being blind and yet insisting that you can see.
Such people do not repent; do not seek the light; do not receive Jesus.
So sin remains within them.
Often people’s greatest problem is not weakness but:
not admitting that they need God.
This is also why:
sinners find it easier to believe; the self-righteous find it hardest to accept the gospel.
Because:
those who know they are blind will look for light; those who think they have light will reject it.
This passage reminds us of five things:
First, Jesus came to bring light into people’s lives. And light reveals a person’s true spiritual condition.
Second, those who can truly see are those who admit they need God. Humility is the beginning of receiving light.
Third, the greatest spiritual blindness is thinking you can see. Pride keeps people from receiving the truth.
Fourth, the people God finds hardest to heal are not the weak but the self-righteous. Because the self-righteous do not feel they need grace.
Fifth, true wisdom is to admit every day that we need the light of Jesus. Apart from the Lord, we will all fall into darkness again.
q: Is there some spiritual pride in you that makes you think you already “see very clearly”?
Today, are you willing to humbly come to Jesus once again and ask Him to enlighten you?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, guard our hearts so that we do not fall into the pride of the Pharisees. Let us always stay humble and admit that we need Your light. Open our spiritual eyes every day, so that we do not merely know a lot on the outside, but truly know You and follow You. May the light of Jesus always shine on our lives. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, amen.

v: “Most certainly, I tell you, one who doesn’t enter by the door into the sheep fold, but climbs up some other way, is a thief and a robber.
But one who enters in by the door is the shepherd of the sheep.
The gatekeeper opens the gate for him, and the sheep listen to his voice. He calls his own sheep by name, and leads them out.
Whenever he brings out his own sheep, he goes before them, and the sheep follow him, for they know his voice.
They will by no means follow a stranger, but will flee from him; for they don’t know the voice of strangers.”
Jesus spoke this parable to them, but they didn’t understand what he was telling them.
b: This passage is the beginning of Jesus’ famous teaching on the “Good Shepherd.” And the background is very important—
Chapter 9 had just ended, with the Pharisees throwing the man who had been blind and now saw out of the synagogue.
Those who should have shepherded the people had no love, no truth, and no compassion.
So Jesus began to reveal:
who the true shepherd is, and who the false ones are.
At the start, Jesus said:
“He who doesn’t enter by the door into the sheepfold, but climbs up some other way, the same is a thief and a robber.”
In those days a sheepfold usually had one proper entrance. The true shepherd goes in by the door; only a thief sneaks over the wall.
Jesus was saying:
True leadership from God is open, above-board, and in line with God’s heart; false spiritual leaders are actually stealing sheep.
On the outside they look like shepherds, but in fact they are for themselves.
The marks of a thief are:
using the sheep; controlling the sheep; harming the sheep; taking the sheep; not loving the sheep.
But the true shepherd is different.
Verse 2 says:
“But he who enters in by the door is the shepherd of the sheep.”
Jesus is the true shepherd who comes from the Father. He does not steal people; He was sent to save them.
True shepherding that belongs to God is not control, but leading lives into God.
Then Jesus said:
“The sheep hear his voice.”
This sentence is very important.
Those who truly belong to the Lord recognize the Lord’s voice.
Not by outward control; not by religious pressure; not by intimidation.
But by:
a real knowledge of the Lord in their lives.
The sheep may not know much, but they recognize the shepherd’s voice.
In the same way, those who truly belong to God are stirred inside by the truth, and respond to the voice of Jesus.
Then Jesus said:
“He calls his own sheep by name.”
This sentence is very tender.
In Jesus’ eyes, we are not a faceless sheep in the flock.
He knows us; knows our names; knows our weakness; knows our tears; knows our life story.
This world often treats people as numbers, tools, and functions, but Jesus knows His sheep by name.
True shepherding is not just managing a group; it is a relationship of life.
Then the Scripture says:
“he goes before them, and the sheep follow him.”
Jesus does not stand behind with a whip to drive the sheep; He goes ahead and leads the way.
True leadership from God is not domination but example.
Jesus Himself first walked the road of the cross; first denied Himself; first obeyed; first loved.
So the sheep are willing to follow Him.
Because a true shepherd does not just give orders; he lives out the way.
Then verse 5 says:
“They will by no means follow a stranger.”
Those who truly belong to the Lord begin to have discernment inside.
The world has many voices:
the voice of fear; the voice of accusation; the voice of pride; the voice of selfish desire; the voice of men; the voice of religious control.
But the Lord’s sheep slowly learn to discern:
which voice sounds like Jesus, and which does not.
Because the voice of Jesus carries:
truth; peace; life; love; holiness; light.
Finally, verse 6 says:
“They did not understand.”
This again shows:
Without a humble heart, even if Jesus Himself speaks, people may not understand.
Spiritual truth is understood not through cleverness but through willingness to follow.
This passage reminds us of five things:
First, a true shepherd who belongs to God leads people closer to God, not controls them. The thief is for himself; the shepherd is for the sheep.
Second, Jesus is the true Good Shepherd. He came from the Father and lays down His life for the sheep.
Third, those who truly belong to the Lord recognize the Lord’s voice. In their lives they respond to the truth.
Fourth, Jesus knows each sheep by name. You are not someone overlooked.
Fifth, true leadership is not domination but example. Jesus Himself walks in front.
q: Whose voice do you listen to most each day right now? The world’s? Your emotions’? Or the Lord’s?
Do you truly believe that Jesus knows you and is leading your life?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You for making Jesus our Good Shepherd. Let us grow more and more familiar with Your voice and not be deceived by the voices of the world and of darkness. And heal the places in us that were wounded by wrong shepherding, so that we may again experience Your real love and leading. May we follow You alone all our lives. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, amen.

v: Jesus therefore said to them again, “Most certainly, I tell you, I am the sheep’s door.
All who came before me are thieves and robbers, but the sheep didn’t listen to them.
I am the door. If anyone enters in by me, he will be saved, and will go in and go out, and will find pasture.
The thief only comes to steal, kill, and destroy. I came that they may have life, and may have it abundantly.
b: This passage is one of Jesus’ most important declarations:
“I am the sheep’s door.”
He is not only the one who shows the way; He Himself is the only entrance.
True life, salvation, peace, and abundance must all come through Jesus.
The Scripture begins with Jesus saying:
“I am the door of the sheep.”
In the sheepfolds of that time, the shepherd would often sleep right at the entrance at night. In other words:
the shepherd himself became the door.
If the sheep wanted to go in or out, they had to pass through the shepherd.
In the same way, Jesus was saying:
The only way to enter the kingdom of God, to receive life, and to be restored to relationship with the Father is through Him.
He is not “one of the ways”; He is the only door.
Many people today think they can enter eternal life:
by good works; by religion; by spiritual practice; by philosophy; by their own effort.
But Jesus said:
“I am the door.”
Because only He can deal with sin; only He can restore people’s relationship with God; only He laid down His life for people; only He rose from the dead.
Then He said:
“All who came before me are thieves and robbers.”
Jesus was not denying the Old Testament prophets; He was pointing to those leaders who falsely claimed to belong to God but did not come from God.
On the outside they talked about God, but in fact they were:
using people; controlling people; taking people; and keeping people away from true life.
True leadership from God brings people to Jesus; false leadership brings people to itself.
Then verse 9 is very precious:
“If anyone enters in by me, he will be saved.”
This is an enormous promise.
Not:
may be saved; saved by effort; saved by luck.
But:
“will be saved.”
Because salvation does not depend on human merit but on the work Jesus has completed.
Those who truly believe and enter into Christ receive:
forgiveness; eternal life; reconciliation with the Father; new life.
Then Jesus said:
“and will go in and go out, and will find pasture.”
This means:
peace; provision; freedom; security; shepherding.
If the sheep have a true shepherd, they do not have to live in constant fear.
Many people look successful on the outside but have never had peace inside.
Because true security is not money, ability, or status, but:
whether we are in the Lord.
Then in verse 10 Jesus draws a complete contrast between two sources of life:
“The thief only comes to steal, kill, and destroy.”
Satan’s work has never changed.
He will:
steal people’s peace; steal people’s purity; steal people’s hope; steal people’s relationships; steal people’s lives; and finally bring destruction.
Sin seems sweet at first, but in the end brings emptiness and death.
Many voices in the world seem to offer freedom, but are actually stealing people’s lives.
But Jesus went on to say:
“I came that they may have life.”
Jesus came not only so that people could “go to heaven,” but so that they could begin to have life right now.
True life is:
being connected to God; having light inside; having peace; love; direction; hope; and the presence of the Holy Spirit.
Then He said:
“and that they may have it abundantly.”
Abundance is not luxury; it is not everything going smoothly; it is not the absence of difficulty.
True abundance is:
having peace inside even in the storm; having contentment inside even in lack; having hope inside even in tears; having a firm foundation for life even when the world changes.
Because true abundance is Christ Himself.
This passage reminds us of five things:
First, Jesus is not one of the ways; He is the only door. True life can only be entered through Him.
Second, false leadership drains, controls, and uses people. The true shepherd leads people into life.
Third, salvation is not earned by effort but freely given by Jesus. Those who enter Christ will surely be saved.
Fourth, Satan’s real work is to steal, kill, and destroy. Sin always ends in death.
Fifth, Jesus came to give people truly abundant life. True abundance is having the life of Christ inside.
q: What things in your life right now are stealing your peace and your life?
Have you truly entered through the door of Jesus, and are you living in His abundant life?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You for making Jesus the door of our life. Keep us, so that the voices of the world and of darkness do not steal our life. And cause us to truly abide in Christ, experiencing the peace, provision, and abundance that come from You. May we follow You alone all our lives and live in Your life. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, amen.

v: I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.
He who is a hired hand, and not a shepherd, who doesn’t own the sheep, sees the wolf coming, leaves the sheep, and flees. The wolf snatches the sheep, and scatters them.
The hired hand flees because he is a hired hand, and doesn’t care for the sheep.
b: This passage shows us:
Jesus is not only a shepherd; He is the good shepherd who is willing to lay down His life for the sheep.
And Jesus also draws a strong contrast between the true shepherd and the “hired hand.”
The biggest difference is not ability, but:
whether he truly loves the sheep.
Jesus first declared:
“I am the good shepherd.”
In the Old Testament, God often described Himself as a shepherd. Psalm 23 says:
“Yahweh is my shepherd.”
Ezekiel 34 also tells how God rebuked the false shepherds who cared only for themselves, and promised that He Himself would come to shepherd the flock.
Now Jesus said directly:
“I am the good shepherd.”
He was declaring:
that He is the Lord whom God promised would truly come to shepherd His people.
And “good” means more than kind; it also carries the sense of:
genuine; beautiful; complete; in line with God’s heart.
He is not a false shepherd; not a shepherd who uses the sheep; not a shepherd who only talks and does not act.
Then Jesus said the most central sentence:
“The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.”
This is the key to the whole passage.
The world’s leaders often ask others to sacrifice for them; but Jesus:
sacrifices Himself for the sheep.
He does not use the sheep to protect Himself; He uses Himself to protect the sheep.
This is the cross.
Jesus was not forced to die; He willingly laid down His life.
Because true love is not just spoken with the mouth; it is willing to pay the price.
Then Jesus began the contrast:
“He who is a hired hand, and not a shepherd.”
The biggest difference between a hired hand and a shepherd is that:
the sheep are not his own.
The hired hand works for wages; the shepherd shepherds out of love.
So in times of peace they look much alike, but when danger comes, the truth is revealed.
Jesus said:
“sees the wolf coming, and leaves the sheep, and flees.”
Because the one he protects first is himself.
The wolf represents:
danger; attack; Satan; temptation; affliction; persecution.
When the cost comes, the false shepherd leaves.
Often people may follow God with a “hired hand mentality” too:
they follow when there are blessings; serve when there are benefits; love the Lord when there is peace.
But when pressure, loss, or injustice comes, they draw back.
Because at the core it is still “myself.”
But Jesus is different.
When the wolf comes, He does not run away; He stands in front of the sheep.
A true shepherd shields the sheep from danger.
So the Scripture says:
“the wolf snatches the sheep, and scatters them.”
Without the protection of a true shepherd, sheep are easily scattered, wounded, and lost.
The world today is the same.
Many people:
have no direction; have no peace; live in fear; are bound by sin; are devoured by the world.
Because they have left the true shepherd.
Finally Jesus said:
“The hired hand flees because he is a hired hand, and doesn’t care for the sheep.”
This sentence points to the most fundamental problem:
It is not a question of ability but a question of love.
True shepherding is not just duty but love in the life.
Jesus cares for the sheep.
He knows the sheep’s weakness; knows their wounds; knows they wander; knows they need protection.
So He is willing to lay down His life.
This passage reminds us of five things:
First, Jesus is the true good shepherd. He does not use the sheep; He lays down His life for them.
Second, true love will always pay a price. The cross is the deepest love.
Third, a crisis reveals a person’s true life. The hired hand runs when he sees the wolf; the true shepherd stands.
Fourth, a life without the Lord is easily devoured and scattered by the world. Only Jesus can truly protect a life.
Fifth, true service that belongs to God is not for profit but out of love. Love is the very core of shepherding.
q: Is your following of God right now out of love, or does it stay at a “hired hand mentality”?
When life brings pressure and cost, are you still willing to follow the good shepherd?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You for giving Jesus to be our good shepherd. Thank You that You did not abandon us but were willing to lay down Your life for us. Let us know Your love more and more, and remove from us the hired-hand mentality, so that we do not live only for ourselves but truly learn the self-denying life of Jesus. May we follow You, our good shepherd, closely all our lives. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, amen.

v: I am the good shepherd. I know my own, and I’m known by my own;
even as the Father knows me, and I know the Father. I lay down my life for the sheep.
I have other sheep, which are not of this fold. I must bring them also, and they will hear my voice. They will become one flock with one shepherd.
Therefore the Father loves me, because I lay down my life,  that I may take it again.
No one takes it away from me, but I lay it down by myself. I have power to lay it down, and I have power to take it again. I received this commandment from my Father.”
b: This passage is full of deep love and security. Jesus does not manage the flock from a distance; between Him and the sheep there is a real, intimate relationship of life.
And the heart of the whole passage is:
Jesus does not love us reluctantly; He willingly lays down His life for us.
The Scripture begins with Jesus saying again:
“I am the good shepherd.”
He is not a shepherd who only teaches principles; not a shepherd who only gives orders; not a shepherd who only watches from afar.
He is:
a shepherd who truly enters into the lives of the sheep.
Then He said:
“I know my own, and I am known by my own.”
The “knowing” here is not merely knowing names, but a deep relationship of life.
Jesus knows:
our weaknesses; our struggles; our tears; our fears; our hidden wounds; the pain we have never spoken.
Sometimes people do not understand us; even those closest to us may misunderstand us.
But Jesus knows completely.
And He does not know coldly; He knows in love.
Then He said:
“and I am known by my own.”
Those who truly belong to the Lord gradually become more and more familiar with Jesus.
Not only knowing some doctrines, but:
recognizing His voice; knowing His heart; experiencing His love; trusting His leading.
What is most precious in faith is not religious form but a real relationship with the Lord.
Then Jesus said:
“even as the Father knows me, and I know the Father.”
This sentence is very deep.
Jesus’ relationship with us is compared to His relationship with the Father.
It means:
the Lord does not treat us casually; He brings us into a relationship of love.
Then He said again:
“I lay down my life for the sheep.”
This sentence is repeated many times in this passage.
Because:
the cross was not an accident; not a failure; not something forced upon Him.
It was Jesus’ willing love.
True love always carries self-denial.
Many say they love but are unwilling to pay the price; but Jesus’ love is:
willing to shed blood for the sheep.
Then verse 16 is very important:
“I have other sheep, which are not of this fold.”
This refers to the Gentiles.
The Jews had thought:
that salvation belonged only to them.
But Jesus said:
there are more sheep.
God’s heart has never been to save only one nation, but:
all peoples.
So Jesus said:
“they will hear my voice.”
Those who truly belong to the Lord, regardless of background, nationality, or culture, will respond to the voice of Jesus.
Finally:
“and they will become one flock with one shepherd.”
True unity does not come through systems; does not come through control; does not come through people.
True unity comes because everyone follows the same shepherd—Jesus.
Apart from Christ, it is hard for people to be truly united; because the self in each person conflicts with others.
Only in Jesus can people truly become one flock.
Then Jesus said:
“Therefore the Father loves me, because I lay down my life, that I may take it again.”
The Father delights in Jesus, because He obeyed completely.
The cross is not a tragedy; it is the most glorious display of the love of obedience.
Then verse 18 is stunning:
“No one takes it away from me, but I lay it down by myself.”
Jesus was not defeated by people; He laid down His life on His own initiative.
He was not powerless when He was seized; He willingly obeyed the Father.
He even said:
“I have power to lay it down, and I have power to take it again.”
This is a declaration of the resurrection.
Death cannot defeat Him; the cross is not the end; He is the Lord of life.
This passage reminds us of five things:
First, Jesus’ relationship with us is real and intimate. He truly knows His sheep.
Second, true faith is not religious form but a relationship with the Lord. The sheep recognize the shepherd’s voice.
Third, Jesus’ love is a self-giving love. The cross was His willing choice.
Fourth, God’s salvation is prepared for all peoples. All who hear the Lord’s voice can come to Him.
Fifth, true unity comes from one shepherd. Only in Christ can people truly be one.
q: Is your relationship with Jesus right now stuck at religion, or is it a real, intimate knowing?
Do you truly believe that Jesus is the good shepherd who willingly laid down His life for you?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You for loving us to the end through Jesus. Thank You that You do not watch us from afar but truly know us and shepherd us. Let us grow more familiar with Your voice and experience Your love more deeply. And remove from us pride and separation, so that in Christ we may truly be one and follow this good shepherd alone. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, amen.

v: Therefore a division arose again among the Jews because of these words.
Many of them said, “He has a demon, and is insane! Why do you listen to him?”
Others said, “These are not the sayings of one possessed by a demon. It isn’t possible for a demon to open the eyes of the blind, is it?”
b: This passage is short, yet it shows very truly that Jesus’ words cause people to divide.
Some are drawn by His words; some are offended by His words; some draw near to the light; some reject the light.
The truth has never been only about making people comfortable; it also exposes what is truly in the heart.
The Scripture begins:
“There was a division again among the Jews because of these words.”
Notice, it says “again.”
From the earlier part of John until now, every time Jesus spoke the truth, the crowd began to divide.
Because Jesus did not come to please people but to reveal the truth.
And when the truth appears, people’s hearts are naturally exposed.
It is the same today.
The same message:
leads some to repent when they hear it; moves some when they hear it; makes others feel offended.
The problem is not that God’s word has changed, but that people’s hearts are different.
Then verse 20 says:
“Many of them said, ‘He has a demon, and is mad!’”
This is a very serious insult.
Jesus had just finished speaking about:
the good shepherd; laying down His life for the sheep; being one with the Father; giving life; knowing the sheep.
But some not only did not accept it, they said:
“He is mad.” “He has a demon.”
This once again shows:
When the truth goes beyond human understanding, if people are unwilling to surrender, they begin to deny, attack, and insult.
Often a message truly from God is not necessarily welcomed by the world.
Because the truth tears down people’s pride and sovereignty.
So these people said:
“Why do you listen to him?”
It meant:
“Stop listening.” “He’s not normal.” “He’s not worth following.”
One of the greatest works of darkness is to make people stop hearing the Lord’s voice.
Because:
as long as people are still willing to listen, there is still a possibility of being enlightened.
Yet in verse 21 another group appears:
“These are not the sayings of one possessed by a demon.”
Though these people did not yet fully believe, at least they were willing to think honestly.
They began to see that:
Jesus’ words were not like darkness; His work was not like evil; what He brought was life, light, and healing.
Then they said:
“Can a demon open the eyes of the blind?”
This is a key sentence.
When it is truly God’s work, even if people are unwilling to admit it, it is hard to deny completely.
Because:
darkness does not truly bring light; Satan does not truly give people life; evil does not truly bring people closer to God.
What Jesus did was not only miracles but restoration:
life; hope; light; relationship with God.
So those who were honest began to waver:
“If He were not from God, how could He do these things?”
This passage shows us that:
People’s attitude toward Jesus reveals the true direction of their lives.
Some only want to protect their own ideas; others are willing to let the truth change them.
They heard the same Jesus, yet the results were completely different.
This passage reminds us of five things:
First, the truth brings division. Not everyone will accept Jesus.
Second, if people are unwilling to surrender, they easily deny and attack the truth. Pride makes people take light for darkness.
Third, what darkness fears most is people continuing to hear the Lord’s voice. Because God’s word can enlighten the heart.
Fourth, honest people, even if they do not yet fully believe, are willing to face the facts. This is an important start in drawing near to the light.
Fifth, work that truly comes from God brings life, healing, and light. Because God’s very nature is life.
q: When God’s word challenges you, is your first reaction to resist, or to keep listening?
Are you willing to be someone who faces the truth honestly and draws near to the light?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, guard our hearts so that we do not reject the truth out of pride. Give us an honest, tender spirit, so that we are willing to keep listening to Your voice, and to surrender even when the truth challenges us. And let us discern work that truly comes from You, and follow You boldly. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, amen.

v: It was the Feast of the Dedication at Jerusalem.
It was winter, and Jesus was walking in the temple, in Solomon’s porch.
The Jews therefore came around him and said to him, “How long will you hold us in suspense? If you are the Christ, tell us plainly.”
Jesus answered them, “I told you, and you don’t believe. The works that I do in my Father’s name, these testify about me.
But you don’t believe, because you are not of my sheep, as I told you.
b: This passage shows us:
People’s greatest problem is not that they do not know the answer, but that they are unwilling to believe it.
Many people think:
“If God were a little clearer, I would believe.” But in fact, what truly holds people back is not lack of evidence but a heart unwilling to surrender.
The Scripture begins by mentioning:
“It was the Feast of the Dedication at Jerusalem. It was winter.”
The Feast of Dedication was the Jewish festival commemorating the cleansing and rededication of the temple.
The irony is:
while people were celebrating the restoration of the temple, the true temple—Jesus—stood before them, and they did not recognize Him.
This is also the condition of people:
outwardly zealous about religion, yet inwardly not truly knowing God.
Then the Scripture says:
“Jesus was walking in the temple, in Solomon’s porch.”
It was winter, and also a time when Jesus was drawing ever nearer to the cross.
And the Jews gathered around Him and asked:
“If you are the Christ, tell us plainly.”
On the surface it looked like they were seeking an answer, but in fact they had heard it many times already.
Jesus had said:
that He is the bread of life; the light of the world; the good shepherd; the one who came down from heaven; one with the Father.
He had also done many miracles:
healing the sick; casting out demons; giving sight to the blind; raising the dead (about to happen).
The problem was not that Jesus was not clear enough, but that:
they were unwilling to accept it.
Often people do not lack light but lack a heart willing to surrender.
Then Jesus answered:
“I told you, and you don’t believe.”
This sentence is very heavy.
What Jesus was really saying was:
“The problem is not that I haven’t said it, but that you don’t believe.”
Unbelief is not only a problem of the mind; often it is a question of who is sovereign over one’s life.
Because if Jesus truly is the Christ, people must:
repent; surrender; step down from being king of their own lives.
And the old self is most unwilling to give up the throne.
Then Jesus said:
“The works that I do in my Father’s name, these testify about me.”
Jesus did not only speak with His mouth; He also proved Himself by His life and works.
What He did:
brought healing; brought light; brought life; brought restoration.
All of these show that He came from the Father.
Work that truly comes from God will always show God’s character.
Yet Jesus finally pointed out the real reason:
“But you don’t believe, because you are not my sheep.”
This sentence is profound.
It is not that they did not believe for lack of evidence; it is that their lives did not belong to the Lord, and so they rejected the Lord.
The Lord’s true sheep respond to Jesus inside; even if they do not fully understand yet, they are drawn by the truth.
But if people insist on living in their own kingdom, even with Jesus standing before them, they still refuse.
This passage reminds us of five things:
First, people’s greatest problem is not lack of answers but unwillingness to believe. Often the light is already enough.
Second, religious zeal is not the same as truly knowing God. People may celebrate the temple yet reject the true Lord.
Third, Jesus testifies of Himself not only with words but with His life and works. What He did shows that He came from the Father.
Fourth, the root of unbelief is often the old self’s unwillingness to surrender. People’s greatest struggle is “who is king.”
Fifth, those who truly belong to the Lord respond to the Lord’s voice. Because sheep recognize the shepherd’s voice.
q: Are there areas where you already know God’s will but are still unwilling to surrender?
Do you truly respond to Jesus’ voice, and not only stay at “knowing”?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, remove from us the hard and unbelieving heart. Do not let us stay at religious knowledge and outward zeal, but truly be willing to believe in and follow Jesus. And make us truly Your sheep, sensitive to Your voice, willing to obey Your leading. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, amen.

v: My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me.
I give eternal life to them. They will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of my hand.
My Father who has given them to me is greater than all. No one is able to snatch them out of my Father’s hand.
I and the Father are one.”
b: This passage is full of deep security and love. Jesus does not only tell us how to follow Him; He also lets us see that:
Those who truly belong to the Lord are held tightly by the Lord.
The world is full of insecurity:
people change; circumstances change; relationships change; bodies grow weak; money is lost; the world shakes.
But here Jesus gives His sheep an enormous promise:
“You are in my hand.”
The Scripture begins with Jesus saying:
“My sheep hear my voice.”
Those who truly belong to the Lord respond to Jesus in their lives.
Not that they have no weakness; not that they never fall; but that inside there is a life that:
wants to draw near to the Lord; wants to hear the Lord; wants to follow the Lord.
The sheep’s greatest trait is not running fast but recognizing the shepherd’s voice.
Then Jesus said:
“I know them.”
This sentence again brings deep comfort.
Often people feel:
no one truly understands me; no one knows my struggles; no one understands my pain.
But Jesus says:
“I know you.”
He does not merely know from afar; He understands deeply.
He knows:
your weakness; your tears; your fears; your failures; your struggles in the night.
And He does not leave after knowing; He still loves you.
Then Jesus said:
“and they follow me.”
True sheep do not only hear; they follow.
Faith is not only listening to sermons; not knowledge; not feeling moved.
True faith produces following.
Sometimes we fall; sometimes we are weak; but the direction is still:
following Jesus.
Then verse 28 is a most precious promise:
“I give eternal life to them.”
Notice, it says “give.”
Eternal life is not earned by human effort; not gained by accumulating merit; not bought by performance.
Eternal life is a gift freely given by Jesus.
And eternal life is not only going to heaven after death; it begins right now:
being connected to God; having the Lord’s life inside; having an eternal hope.
Then Jesus said:
“They will never perish.”
This is not because the sheep are great, but because the shepherd is reliable.
What truly keeps us is not the strength with which we hold on to God, but:
God holding on to us.
Then Jesus said:
“and no one will snatch them out of my hand.”
This sentence is full of power.
Many things in the world want to snatch us away:
sin; temptation; fear; accusation; affliction; Satan; circumstances.
But Jesus said:
“No one.”
Because the one who truly holds the sheep is the Lord Himself.
Then He said again:
“No one is able to snatch them out of my Father’s hand.”
Here there is a double protection:
in Jesus’ hand; and also in the Father’s hand.
And:
“My Father, who has given them to me, is greater than all.”
It means:
no power is greater than God.
The world will shake; kingdoms will change; people will fail; but God always reigns.
Finally, verse 30:
“I and the Father are one.”
This is an extremely important declaration.
Jesus is not an ordinary prophet; not merely someone who represents God.
He and the Father are one.
He has God’s authority; God’s life; God’s power; God’s nature.
Therefore He can truly keep His sheep forever.
This passage reminds us of five things:
First, those who truly belong to the Lord hear the Lord’s voice and follow Him. Direction matters more than perfection.
Second, Jesus truly knows His sheep. He knows all your circumstances.
Third, eternal life is grace freely given by Jesus. It is not earned by people.
Fourth, what truly keeps us is not how great we are but God’s hand. No one can snatch away those who belong to the Lord.
Fifth, Jesus and the Father are one. He is truly God, with complete power and authority.
q: Where is your true security built right now?
Are you still willing each day to hear the Lord’s voice and follow Him?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You for giving us eternal life and true security through Jesus. When the world is full of unrest and shaking, let us know that we are in Your hand. And help us hear Your voice every day and follow Your footsteps, never leaving You, our good shepherd. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, amen.

v: Therefore Jews took up stones again to stone him.
Jesus answered them, “I have shown you many good works from my Father. For which of those works do you stone me?”
The Jews answered him, “We don’t stone you for a good work, but for blasphemy: because you, being a man, make yourself God.”
b: This passage shows us something worth pondering:
Seeing the same Jesus, some worship Him, while others want to kill Him.
The man born blind in chapter 9 finally fell down and worshiped Jesus; but these religious leaders in chapter 10 picked up stones to stone Him.
The problem is not that Jesus is different, but that people’s hearts are different.
The Scripture begins:
“Therefore Jews took up stones again to stone him.”
Notice the word “again.”
This was not the first time.
From the beginning of John, the more clearly Jesus revealed His identity, the more fiercely those who opposed Him reacted.
The brighter the light, the stronger the reaction of the darkness.
Because the truth not only brings comfort; it also challenges the throne inside people.
When Jesus said:
“I and the Father are one.”
He had clearly declared His deity.
And this is exactly what they could not accept.
Why?
Because if Jesus truly is God, then people can no longer continue to be their own king.
Many people are not unable to accept that God exists; they are unwilling to accept that God reigns.
Then Jesus asked an interesting question:
“I have shown you many good works from my Father. For which of those works do you stone me?”
Jesus did not first defend Himself; He brought the focus back to the facts.
What had He done?
Healed the sick; opened the eyes of the blind; made the lame walk; fed the crowds; set free those who were bound.
All that He did was good works.
In other words:
If we look at the fruit, Jesus clearly came from God.
Those who truly come from God will surely show God’s character in their lives.
Yet human prejudice is sometimes stronger than the facts.
When people have decided to reject the truth, no amount of evidence can persuade them.
So the Jews answered:
“We don’t stone you for a good work, but for blasphemy.”
They had actually admitted:
that what Jesus did were good works.
But the problem was not the good works but His identity.
Then they said:
“because you, being a man, make yourself God.”
This sentence is very important.
Because it proves that:
they understood perfectly what Jesus meant.
Some say:
Jesus never claimed to be God.
But that is not so.
From the Jews’ reaction we can tell that they knew very well that Jesus was declaring Himself equal with the Father.
That is why they considered it “blasphemy.”
Yet the real problem was not that Jesus had said something wrong.
It was that:
they did not believe who He is.
If Jesus were not God, it would indeed be blasphemy.
But if Jesus truly is God, then those who reject Him are rejecting God.
So the whole Gospel keeps asking the same question:
Who do you say Jesus is?
A teacher? A prophet? A religious figure? Or the Son of God?
This question determines a person’s eternal direction.
Because the very heart of faith is not first asking:
how many good works you have done; how much theology you know; how many meetings you attend.
But:
how you respond to Jesus.
This passage reminds us of five things:
First, Jesus’ identity is always a question people must face. We cannot treat Him merely as a great man.
Second, the brighter the light, the stronger the reaction of the darkness may be. The truth often challenges people’s pride.
Third, if people have already decided to reject God, no amount of evidence can persuade them. The problem is often not the mind but the heart.
Fourth, Jesus’ life was full of good works and grace. All that He did reveals the Father’s glory.
Fifth, the core of true faith is not religion but who Jesus is. Knowing Him determines the direction of our lives.
q: In your heart, who exactly is Jesus?
Do you truly treat Him as the Lord of your life, and not merely one part of your faith?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You for revealing Yourself to us through Jesus. Remove from us all pride and prejudice, so that we do not merely admire Jesus but truly believe in Him and follow Him. And let us know every day more deeply that He is the Son of God and the Lord of life, so that we are willing to hand the sovereignty of our lives completely over to Him. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, amen.

v: Jesus answered them, “Isn’t it written in your law, ‘I said, you are gods?’
If he called them gods, to whom the word of God came (and the Scripture can’t be broken),
do you say of him whom the Father sanctified and sent into the world, ‘You blaspheme,’ because I said, ‘I am the Son of God?’
b: At first glance this passage may seem hard to understand, but in fact Jesus was using the Scriptures the Jews knew best to answer their accusation against Him.
The Jews had just said:
“You, being a man, make yourself God.”
Jesus did not immediately get angry, nor did He silence them with power,
but brought them back to Scripture.
This also shows us an important principle:
The basis of truth is not human feeling but God’s word.
Jesus quoted Psalm 82:6:
“I said, ‘You are gods, all of you sons of the Most High.’”
The “gods” here does not mean that people really become deities, but refers to those who were given authority by God to represent Him in carrying out judgment and rule.
In Hebrew culture, judges, leaders, and rulers, because they received God’s authority, were sometimes called representatives of “God” (Elohim).
What Jesus meant was:
If in the Old Testament those who were limited, sinful, and who received God’s word could in some sense be called “gods,”
then:
why can’t the Son of God, whom the Father consecrated and sent into the world Himself, call Himself the Son of God?
In other words,
Jesus was not lowering His identity; He was pointing out a contradiction in their argument.
He was saying:
“Even your own Scriptures allow such a use. Why are you so angry with me?”
Then Jesus said something very important:
“the Scripture cannot be broken.”
This is one of Jesus’ clearest declarations of the authority of Scripture.
“Cannot be broken” in the original means:
cannot be annulled; cannot be overturned; cannot become void.
Jesus fully believed:
that God’s word is always valid.
Even if heaven and earth change, human culture changes, and the times change,
God’s word still stands.
Today many want to revise the truth to fit the world, but Jesus reminds us:
It is not that God’s word adapts to the world,
but that people should return to God’s word.
Because:
human thinking changes; social values change; popular opinion changes;
only God’s truth never changes.
Then Jesus said:
“him whom the Father sanctified and sent into the world.”
This sentence reveals His identity.
“Sanctified” means:
specially chosen by God; wholly belonging to God; bearing God’s mission.
And “sent into the world” shows that:
Jesus was not a religious figure who happened to be born;
He was sent by the Father.
He did not come to found a religion,
but to accomplish salvation.
Therefore,
He was not exalting Himself;
He was fulfilling the mission the Father entrusted to Him.
This also makes us think of our own lives.
Although every Christian does not have Jesus’ unique identity as Son of God,
we too are:
people set apart as holy by God; people sent by God into the world.
We live not only for ourselves,
but to fulfill what God has entrusted to us.
As the 321 principles remind us:
Jesus is the example; the Bible is the standard of truth; the Holy Spirit is the guide.
The greatest value in life
is not building our own kingdom,
but accomplishing God’s will.
This passage reminds us of five things:
First, the basis of truth is God’s word, not human feeling. Jesus always returned to Scripture.
Second, God’s word is always valid. Heaven and earth will change, but the truth never changes.
Third, Jesus is not an ordinary man. He is the Son of God whom the Father sanctified and sent into the world.
Fourth, those who truly know Jesus come to understand His identity more and more. He is not only a teacher but the Savior.
Fifth, we too are people set apart by God. Our lives have a mission, a calling, and a direction.
q: Is your standard for judging life God’s word or human opinion?
Do you clearly know that you are someone set apart as holy by God and sent into the world?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You for giving us truth that never changes. Let us be like Jesus, returning to Your word in everything, not going by feelings, not following the world, but building on the foundation of truth. And help us understand our identity and mission, live out a life that belongs to You, and glorify Your name. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, amen.

v: If I don’t do the works of my Father, don’t believe me.
But if I do them, though you don’t believe me, believe the works, that you may know and believe that the Father is in me, and I in the Father.”
They sought again to seize him, and he went out of their hand.
b: This passage shows us an important trait of faith in Jesus:
The truth does not fear examination.
Jesus never asked people to believe in Him blindly. He kept inviting people to:
look at what He did; observe His life; examine His works.
Because what truly comes from God can stand the test.
The Scripture begins with Jesus saying:
“If I don’t do the works of my Father, don’t believe me.”
This sentence is stunning.
Jesus did not say:
“Don’t ask, just believe.”
Instead He said:
“If I am not living out the Father’s works, you don’t have to believe me.”
This is great confidence.
Because He knew that:
His life was in complete agreement with the Father’s will.
The teaching He gave; the miracles He did; His compassion for people; His holiness; His love;
all bear witness that He came from the Father.
For those who truly belong to God, life and message are consistent.
If someone speaks of God with his mouth but his life is full of pride, selfishness, and darkness,
his witness naturally loses its power.
But Jesus is different.
He did not only speak the truth;
He is the truth lived out.
Then Jesus said:
“But if I do them, though you don’t believe me, believe the works.”
It means:
Even if you cannot yet accept who I am,
at least face the facts honestly.
Because the facts are right before you:
the blind see; the lame walk; those possessed are set free; lives are restored.
Jesus did not attract people with slogans,
but with God’s real works.
This also reminds us that:
the most powerful witness to the gospel
is often not debate
but a life.
When a person’s life is changed by Jesus,
that is the most powerful evidence.
Then Jesus said:
“that you may know and understand that the Father is in me, and I in the Father.”
This is the heart of the whole passage.
All of Jesus’ miracles
were not to show off power;
were not to build a personal reputation;
but to reveal:
that He is one with the Father.
His work is the Father’s work; His heart is the Father’s heart; His love is the Father’s love.
When people see Jesus,
they are in fact seeing the Heavenly Father.
That is why John keeps telling us:
to know Jesus is to know God; to receive Jesus is to receive God; to reject Jesus is to reject God.
Yet verse 39 shows another regrettable scene:
“Again they sought to seize him.”
Jesus had given so much evidence,
but they still refused.
This lets us understand one thing:
the deepest root of unbelief
is often not a problem of reason
but a problem of the heart.
When people decide not to accept the light,
no matter how brightly it shines,
they will still close their eyes.
The Pharisees’ problem was not lack of evidence,
but that they were unwilling to give up their thrones.
They were afraid of losing:
authority; status; control; the glory of men.
So they chose to reject Jesus.
Finally the Scripture says:
“but he went out of their hand.”
Not because Jesus was afraid,
but because His time had not yet come.
The whole Gospel of John shows again and again:
Jesus’ life was entirely under the Father’s control.
No one could take His life ahead of time.
When He later went to the cross,
it was not because of failure,
but because of obedience.
This passage reminds us of five things:
First, the truth does not fear examination. Jesus’ life and works prove that He came from God.
Second, true witness is not only words but life. A changed life is the most powerful evidence.
Third, all of Jesus’ works reveal the Heavenly Father. He came to let people know God.
Fourth, the greatest problem in unbelief is often not the mind but the heart. Pride keeps people from receiving the truth.
Fifth, Jesus’ life was entirely in the Father’s timing. No power can stop God’s plan.
q: Is your life bearing witness to Jesus’ real work?
Is there any pride or stubbornness keeping you from knowing the Lord more deeply?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You for revealing Yourself to us through Jesus. Give us a humble, teachable heart, and do not let pride keep us from receiving the truth. And make our lives a witness to the gospel, so that people who see the change in our lives may see Your glory. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, amen.

v: He went away again beyond the Jordan into the place where John was baptizing at first, and he stayed there.
Many came to him. They said, “John indeed did no sign, but everything that John said about this man is true.”
Many believed in him there.
b: This passage is a beautiful ending to John chapter 10.
Earlier we saw:
the religious leaders rejecting Jesus; the Pharisees wanting to seize Jesus; some picking up stones to stone Him.
Yet God’s work did not stop because of this.
Because:
people’s rejection cannot stop God’s plan.
The Scripture begins:
“He went away again beyond the Jordan.”
He left Jerusalem and went to the place where John had first baptized.
This is full of spiritual meaning.
Because this is exactly where Jesus’ public ministry began.
Back then John cried out here:
“Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand.”
And it was here that John testified:
“Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!”
Now Jesus returned to this place again.
It was like a spiritual looking back.
Those who had heard John’s message
now finally saw the One to whom John had pointed.
Then the Scripture says:
“Many came to him.”
This forms a strong contrast with Jerusalem.
In Jerusalem:
some debated; some attacked; some rejected.
But beyond the Jordan:
many were willing to come to Jesus.
This reminds us that:
Those who truly seek God will in the end come to Christ.
Because what people deep down truly need
is not religion
but a Savior.
Then they said:
“John indeed did no sign.”
This is interesting.
John the Baptist did not heal the sick; did not give sight to the blind; did not raise the dead.
He did not perform great miracles as Elijah and Elisha did.
Yet Jesus called him:
“Among those who are born of women there is not a greater prophet than John the Baptizer.”
Why?
Because God’s measure of a person
is not outward achievement
but whether he is faithful to complete his mission.
John’s greatest success
was not performing miracles,
but bringing people to Jesus.
This is the heart of true service.
Not getting people to remember yourself;
but getting people to know Christ.
Then the people said:
“All things whatever John said about this man were true.”
Years had passed,
and they began to discover that:
John’s testimony had been completely fulfilled.
He said Jesus was the Lamb of God;
it was true.
He said Jesus was the Son of God;
it was true.
He said Jesus would baptize with the Holy Spirit;
it was true.
He said he himself must decrease and Jesus must increase;
that was true too.
Time proved John’s faithful testimony.
In the same way,
God’s truth also stands the test of time.
Human theories change;
worldly trends change;
cultural values change;
but God’s word stands forever.
Finally verse 42 says:
“Many believed in him there.”
This is the most beautiful result of the whole passage.
John did not draw people to himself;
he brought them to Jesus.
And when people truly come to know Jesus,
faith is born.
Notice,
they did not believe because they saw miracles.
The Scripture mentions no new miracle.
They believed because of:
John’s testimony; Jesus’ life; Jesus’ words;
that is why they believed in Him.
This shows us that:
miracles can attract people;
but what truly saves people
is still knowing and trusting Jesus.
This passage reminds us of five things:
First, people’s rejection cannot stop God’s work. Even when some oppose, God is still looking for those willing to believe.
Second, those who truly seek God will finally come to Jesus. Because only He has the way of eternal life.
Third, God values faithfulness over outward achievement. John did no miracles, yet he accomplished a great mission.
Fourth, true service is not exalting ourselves but exalting Christ. Bringing people to Jesus is the greatest success.
Fifth, God’s truth stands the test of time. All words that truly come from God will in the end be proved true.
q: Is your life right now exalting yourself, or exalting Jesus?
If others come to know Christ through you, what do you most hope they see?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You for John the Baptist’s faithful witness to Jesus, and thank You for giving us the opportunity to know this Savior. Help us, like John, not to exalt ourselves but to exalt Christ. And make us faithful witnesses who bring more people to Jesus, so that by trusting in the Lord they may receive eternal life. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, amen.

v: Now a certain man was sick, Lazarus from Bethany, of the village of Mary and her sister, Martha.
It was that Mary who had anointed the Lord with ointment and wiped his feet with her hair, whose brother, Lazarus, was sick.
The sisters therefore sent to him, saying, “Lord, behold, he for whom you have great affection is sick.”
But when Jesus heard it, he said, “This sickness is not to death, but for the glory of God, that God’s Son may be glorified by it.”
b: John chapter 11 is an important turning point in the whole Gospel.
Because in this chapter,
Jesus was about to perform one of the greatest miracles of His public ministry—
raising Lazarus from the dead.
And this miracle also directly hastened the religious leaders’ decision to kill Jesus.
Therefore,
this is not only a story of healing,
but also an important revelation about:
life; death; faith; glory;
that it reveals.
The Scripture begins by introducing:
Lazarus was sick.
This was not an unfamiliar family.
Bethany was about three kilometers from Jerusalem,
a place where Jesus often stayed.
Martha, Mary, and Lazarus
were very close friends of Jesus.
In other words:
this was not the suffering of ordinary people,
but suffering experienced by those whom Jesus loved.
This point is very important.
Many people think:
those who love the Lord will not get sick; devout people will not meet difficulty; those whom God loves will not suffer.
But the story of Lazarus tells us:
Those whom the Lord loves can also get sick.
Loving God
does not mean life has no storms;
it means the Lord is with us in the storm.
Verse 3 is very moving.
The two sisters sent word to Jesus,
with no long speech,
saying only one sentence:
“Lord, behold, he whom you love is sick.”
They did not command the Lord;
did not complain to the Lord;
did not analyze the illness;
they simply brought the need to the Lord.
Because they believed that:
Jesus knows;
Jesus cares;
Jesus will take care of it.
This is a model of mature prayer.
Often,
our prayers are as if we were teaching God what to do.
But true faith is:
to hand the need over to the Lord,
trusting that He knows better than we do.
Yet,
Jesus’ answer that followed
surprised everyone.
He said:
“This sickness is not to death.”
Standing in that moment,
this sentence seems hard to understand.
Because Lazarus did in fact die later.
Was Jesus wrong, then?
Of course not.
Because Jesus does not look at things
only as they are in front of us.
People see death;
Jesus sees resurrection.
People see an ending;
Jesus sees glory.
In God’s eyes,
death is not the end.
Because He holds life in His hands.
Then Jesus said:
“but for the glory of God.”
This sentence opens up an important truth:
Some suffering
is not punishment;
is not accident;
but the stage for God’s glorious work.
Of course,
not all suffering can be understood immediately.
But many times,
God allows certain things to happen
because He is going to accomplish something greater.
Joseph sold into Egypt;
Moses forty years in the wilderness;
David hunted by Saul;
Paul facing persecution;
at the time all looked like failure.
But later all became vessels of God’s glory.
Lazarus’ sickness is the same.
If it were only healing,
people would see power;
but if the dead are raised,
people see the glory of God.
So Jesus finally said:
“that God’s Son may be glorified by it.”
The greatest purpose of a miracle
is not to solve people’s problems;
but to reveal who Jesus is.
Because:
He is not only a healer;
He is the Lord of life.
He is not only a helper;
He is the resurrection and the life.
This passage reminds us of five things:
First, those whom the Lord loves also go through suffering. Faith in the Lord does not spare us from storms, but means the Lord walks with us in the storm.
Second, true faith is bringing our needs to the Lord. Trusting that He knows, and trusting that He cares.
Third, people see problems; God sees glory. Our vision often stops at the present, but God sees the outcome.
Fourth, some suffering is the stage for God’s glorious work. God can turn pain into a testimony.
Fifth, Jesus is not only the Lord who heals the sick, but the Lord of life. He holds both life and death.
q: Is there something in your life right now that you do not understand?
Are you willing to believe that the outcome God sees is greater than what you see now?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, when we face illness, difficulty, and circumstances we do not understand, give us faith. Let us learn, like Martha and Mary, to bring our needs to You, trusting that You know, You care, and You reign. Even when we cannot yet see the answer, help us believe that You are accomplishing a greater glory. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, amen.

v: Now Jesus loved Martha, and her sister, and Lazarus.
When therefore he heard that he was sick, he stayed two days in the place where he was.
Then after this he said to the disciples, “Let’s go into Judea again.”
The disciples asked him, “Rabbi, the Jews were just trying to stone you. Are you going there again?”
Jesus answered, “Aren’t there twelve hours of daylight? If a man walks in the day, he doesn’t stumble, because he sees the light of this world.
But if a man walks in the night, he stumbles, because the light isn’t in him.”
b: This passage holds a truth that seems contradictory, yet is utterly precious:
Jesus loved them, and so He did not go right away.
By human logic,
it ought to be:
the more you love, the faster you go; the more you care, the sooner you help.
But John deliberately wrote:
"Now Jesus loved Martha, and her sister, and Lazarus."
And the very next line says:
"when he heard therefore that he was sick, he stayed two days in the place where he was."
This is the most puzzling part of the whole passage.
Mary and Martha must have been waiting:
Surely He will come today; surely tomorrow; surely He should be here by now.
But Jesus did not appear.
Many times,
our own lives have similar experiences.
We prayed;
we cried out;
we believed in God;
but the answer did not come right away.
So we begin to wonder:
Has the Lord forgotten? Does the Lord not care? Has the Lord not heard?
Yet this passage tells us:
Jesus' delay is not Jesus' indifference.
In fact,
it was precisely because He loved them
that He did not act at once.
Because what He wanted to give them
was not just one healing;
but a deeper opportunity to know God.
Many times,
we want God to solve the problem right now;
but God is preparing a greater grace.
We want God to change our circumstances;
but God first wants to change our faith.
We want God to remove the pain at once;
but God wants us to know Him more deeply.
Therefore,
God's timing is often different from man's timing.
Man's focus is:
faster.
God's focus is:
best.
Then in verse 7,
Jesus finally says:
"Let's go into Judea again."
But the disciples immediately grew tense.
Because earlier, in chapter ten,
the Jews had already picked up stones to stone Jesus.
Going back now
meant entering a danger zone.
So the disciples said:
"The Jews were just trying to stone you."
In fact this was not only concern for Jesus,
but concern for themselves.
Because those who follow Jesus
may face danger together with Him.
This shows us that
many times,
the greatest enemy of faith is not circumstances,
but fear.
When people see only the wind and waves,
they forget the Lord who rules the wind and waves.
Then Jesus answered:
"Aren't there twelve hours of daylight?"
He was not talking about astronomy,
but about God's timing.
Jesus knew:
His life was in the Father's hands.
As long as He was within the time the Father had set,
no one could harm Him.
So He said:
"If a man walks in the day, he doesn't stumble."
It means:
when a person lives in God's will,
following God's leading,
he has God's light upon him.
Even when the road is hard,
he can still walk steadily.
What truly protects a person
is not a safe environment;
but the presence of God.
Many people spend their whole lives pursuing "safety,"
yet overlook this:
the greatest security is not circumstances,
but God.
Then Jesus said:
"But if a man walks in the night, he stumbles."
Night stands for:
leaving God's guidance; making decisions on our own; relying on human wisdom; living by fear.
Away from God's light,
even what looks safe
will in the end still stumble.
So Jesus did not return to Judea on impulse,
nor out of recklessness.
He was living in the Father's timing.
And this is the secret of His peace and steadiness throughout His life.
This passage reminds us:
First, God's delay is not God's refusal. Jesus loved them, so He prepared a greater grace.
Second, we value speed; God values completion. God's timing is always better than ours.
Third, fear often hinders us from following God. When we look only at circumstances, faith begins to waver.
Fourth, true security is not circumstances but the presence of God. Those who live in God's will can walk forward with confidence.
Fifth, the greatest wisdom in life is to live in the light of God. Those who follow the Lord will not stumble, even on a hard road.
q: Are you in a season of waiting for God to work?
Are you willing to believe that God's timing, though different, is always the best timing?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, as we wait for You, give us faith. When You seem to delay, help us believe that You are still in control. Keep us from living in fear, and let us live in Your light. May we learn from Jesus to trust Your timing and obey Your leading, knowing that what You arrange is always best. We pray in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, amen.

v: He said these things, and after that, he said to them, “Our friend, Lazarus, has fallen asleep, but I am going so that I may awake him out of sleep.”
The disciples therefore said, “Lord, if he has fallen asleep, he will recover.”
Now Jesus had spoken of his death, but they thought that he spoke of taking rest in sleep.
So Jesus said to them plainly then, “Lazarus is dead.
I am glad for your sakes that I was not there, so that you may believe. Nevertheless, let’s go to him.”
Thomas therefore, who is called Didymus, said to his fellow disciples, “Let’s go also, that we may die with him.”
b: This passage shows us:
Man sees death; Jesus sees resurrection.
Man sees an ending; Jesus sees the beginning of God's glorious work.
At the start, Jesus says:
"Our friend Lazarus has fallen asleep."
This is a special way Jesus describes death.
To the world,
death is:
an end; a loss; despair; something irreversible.
But to Jesus,
death is like sleep.
Not because death is unreal,
but because:
He is Lord over life.
When a mother sees her child asleep,
she does not cry out in despair,
because she knows the child will wake again.
In the same way,
in Jesus' eyes,
the death of one who belongs to God is not disappearing forever,
but a temporary sleep.
This is also why the New Testament so often says "fallen asleep" of believers who die.
Because resurrection is a real hope.
Yet the disciples did not understand.
They said:
"Lord, if he has fallen asleep, he will recover."
They thought:
since he was sleeping,
he must be getting better.
So John adds:
"Now Jesus had spoken of his death, but they thought that he spoke of taking rest in sleep."
This happens often in John's Gospel.
Jesus speaks of spiritual things,
and people listen with earthly understanding.
Nicodemus in chapter three was like this;
the Samaritan woman in chapter four was like this;
the crowds who ate the bread of life in chapter six were like this;
and now the disciples are the same.
Many times,
God is speaking of eternal things,
and we think only of what is in front of us.
God looks at life,
and we look only at circumstances;
God looks at eternity,
and we look only at the present.
So Jesus had to say it plainly:
"Lazarus is dead."
This is the fact.
God never denies reality.
Faith is not pretending there is no problem;
it is not self-comfort;
it is not escaping reality.
Jesus clearly acknowledged:
Lazarus really was dead.
True faith
is not denying death,
but still believing in the midst of death that God reigns.
Then Jesus said something surprising:
"I am glad for your sakes that I was not there."
If we do not read carefully,
this seems hard to understand.
Lazarus has died;
why would Jesus be glad?
Of course He was not glad because Lazarus died.
What Jesus was glad about was this:
through this event, God was about to
bring the disciples into deeper faith.
So He went on:
"to the intent that you may believe."
Many times,
God allows certain circumstances,
not to destroy us,
but to build us up.
Some faith
can only be learned in the storm;
some knowing of God
can only be gained in the dark night;
some breakthroughs in spiritual life
can only happen in a hopeless place.
If Lazarus had only been healed of his sickness,
the disciples would have seen Jesus as the Healer;
but when the dead are raised,
they will know more deeply:
Jesus is the Lord of life.
Then a very interesting figure appears in the text:
Thomas.
He said:
"Let's also go, that we may die with him!"
Many people think of Thomas
only for his later doubt.
But here Thomas is actually courageous.
He knew that going back to Judea was dangerous;
he knew Jesus might be killed;
he himself might be implicated.
Yet he was still willing to go.
Although he did not fully understand what Jesus would do,
he was still willing to follow.
This is the life of a true disciple.
Sometimes
we may not fully understand God's plan;
yet we are still willing to follow.
This is faith.
This passage reminds us:
First, to Jesus death is not the end. He is Lord of life and Lord of resurrection.
Second, we often understand God's words with earthly eyes. We need the Holy Spirit to open our spiritual eyes.
Third, true faith is not denying reality but believing God within reality. Lazarus really was dead, yet God still reigns.
Fourth, some circumstances are used by God to build faith. Suffering is not necessarily failure; it may be preparation for greater glory.
Fifth, true following is to walk with the Lord even when we do not fully understand. Here Thomas shows a side of faithful loyalty.
q: Is there a hope in your life that seems to have already "died"?
Are you willing to believe that Jesus is still the Lord of resurrection and life?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, when we face difficulty and disappointment in life, help us to see not only the death and ending before us, but Your resurrection power. Open our spiritual eyes, so that even in hopeless places we still believe You reign. Give us also a heart of faithful following like Thomas, willing to keep following You even when we do not fully understand. We pray in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, amen.

v: So when Jesus came, he found that he had been in the tomb four days already.
Now Bethany was near Jerusalem, about fifteen stadia away.
Many of the Jews had joined the women around Martha and Mary, to console them concerning their brother.
Then when Martha heard that Jesus was coming, she went and met him, but Mary stayed in the house.
Therefore Martha said to Jesus, “Lord, if you would have been here, my brother wouldn’t have died.
Even now I know that whatever you ask of God, God will give you.”
b: This passage is full of the reality of being human.
This is not a theology classroom,
but a household full of tears.
Death has already happened;
hope seems to have ended;
waiting has turned into disappointment;
faith is beginning to be challenged by reality.
Yet it is in just such a place
that the glory of God is about to be revealed.
The text says:
"Lazarus had been in the tomb four days already."
John specifically records "four days."
This is no casual detail.
In the thinking of the Jews at that time,
when someone had just died,
there might still be a thread of hope;
but by the fourth day,
the body had begun to decay,
and all hope was considered completely over.
In other words,
Lazarus was not just freshly dead;
he was not in a coma;
he was not apparently dead;
he was truly dead.
Human methods had run out;
the doctors had no way;
the family had no way;
the disciples had no way.
It is exactly where people reach the end
that God's work begins.
Many times,
God allows us to come to "the fourth day."
Because if people still have their own way,
they often do not truly depend on God.
The end of man
is often the starting point of God's work.
Then the text mentions:
many Jews had come to comfort Martha and Mary.
This shows that the family was well respected in the area.
Many people kept them company,
but no one could solve their real problem.
Because:
there is a pain
that comfort cannot solve;
only Jesus can.
It is the same today.
The world can give encouragement;
psychology can give methods;
friends can give company;
but only Jesus can give true life.
In verse 20 the two sisters respond differently.
"Martha, when she heard that Jesus was coming, went and met him."
Martha was always a woman of action.
The moment she heard Jesus was coming,
she went out at once.
Mary, however, still sat in the house.
The two had different personalities,
and expressed their grief in different ways.
This shows us:
God accepts different kinds of people.
Some in pain actively seek God;
some weep quietly.
But the Lord understands them both.
He knows the heart of each one.
Then Martha says something full of pain:
"Lord, if you would have been here, my brother wouldn't have died."
In these words there is faith,
and also disappointment.
There is belief,
and also doubt.
She is really saying:
"Lord, I believe You can heal;
but You came too late."
This is also the cry in many people's prayers.
Lord,
if You had worked sooner;
if You had opened the way sooner;
if You had saved sooner;
things would not have turned out like this.
Martha's question
is really our question.
We often believe God has power,
yet doubt God's timing.
We believe God can do it,
but do not understand why He did not do it at once.
Yet
God's greatest work
often does not proceed on the schedule we expect.
Because He sees
more than we do.
Then in verse 22,
Martha says something very precious:
"Even now, I know that, whatever you ask of God, God will give you."
This is the turning point of faith.
Although she did not understand;
although she was grieving;
although she was disappointed;
she still said:
"Even now."
Not yesterday;
not in the past;
not "if only";
but now.
True faith
is not because we understand everything;
it is holding on to God even when we do not understand.
She believed:
even when things have reached their worst,
Jesus still has the answer.
Many times,
what God waits for
is exactly this kind of faith.
Not built on circumstances;
not built on feelings;
but built on God Himself.
This passage reminds us:
First, the place where people reach their end is often where God's work begins. Lazarus had been dead four days, yet God's power was never limited.
Second, the world can give comfort, but only Jesus can give life. True hope is in the Lord.
Third, God accepts people of different temperaments. Whether Martha or Mary, the Lord loved them both.
Fourth, we often believe in God's power but do not understand God's timing. God's delay does not mean God's absence.
Fifth, "Even now" is an important declaration of faith. Even when circumstances have not changed, God still reigns.
q: Are you facing something that feels "already too late"?
Are you willing to say to the Lord, "Even now, I still believe You can work"?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, when we face disappointment and do not understand, help us, like Martha, to still say to You, "Even now, I know." Even when circumstances seem to have no hope left, let us believe that You still reign. Open our eyes to see that Your timing is higher than our timing, and Your ways higher than our ways. We pray in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, amen.

v: Jesus said to her, “Your brother will rise again.”
Martha said to him, “I know that he will rise again in the resurrection at the last day.”
Jesus said to her, “I am the resurrection and the life. He who believes in me will still live, even if he dies.
Whoever lives and believes in me will never die. Do you believe this?”
She said to him, “Yes, Lord. I have come to believe that you are the Christ, God’s Son, he who comes into the world.”
b: This passage is one of the greatest declarations in John's Gospel.
If we say that:
John chapter six is "the bread of life";
chapter eight is "the light of the world";
chapter ten is "the good shepherd";
then in chapter eleven,
Jesus shows us:
He is the resurrection and the life.
This is not merely a theological concept,
but a declaration that changes the destiny of humankind.
At that time Martha was standing in the grief of her brother's death.
She believed in God;
she believed in Jesus;
but her faith still rested in the future.
So Jesus said to her:
"Your brother will rise again."
These were words full of hope.
Yet Martha understood it this way:
"I know that he will rise again in the resurrection at the last day."
She was not wrong.
Among the Jews, the Pharisees believed in the resurrection at the last day.
But what Martha really meant was:
"I know that someday there will be a resurrection,
but right now he is dead."
She placed resurrection in the distant future.
Many Christians are the same.
They believe in heaven;
they believe in eternal life;
they believe in the resurrection;
but these truths seem far from the present.
Yet Jesus then speaks the most central sentence of the whole chapter:
"I am the resurrection and the life."
The original can be understood even more directly as:
"I am the resurrection, I am the life."
Notice,
Jesus did not say:
"I am able to give you resurrection."
He said:
"I am the resurrection."
He did not say:
"I can give life."
He said:
"I am the life."
This is an utterly astonishing declaration.
Because:
resurrection is not a thing;
it is a Lord.
Life is not a kind of power;
it is a Lord.
In other words,
where Jesus is,
there is life;
where Jesus is,
there is the hope of resurrection.
Therefore,
the very center of the Christian faith
is not a set of doctrines,
but Jesus Himself.
Then Jesus said:
"He who believes in me, though he die, yet shall he live."
This speaks of the death of the body.
Believers will still pass away;
they will still experience the end of the physical body;
but death is no longer the last word.
Because Christ has overcome death.
Paul later said:
"Death, where is your victory?"
Death is like a door,
not an end;
but an entrance into eternity.
Therefore,
for the believer,
death is not destruction,
but going home.
Then verse 26:
"Whoever lives and believes in me will never die."
This speaks of another dimension.
The body will die,
but the spiritual life never dies.
Because eternal life does not begin after death,
but from the moment we believe in Jesus.
When a person trusts in Christ,
God's life has already entered him.
Therefore,
even when the body lies in the grave,
that life is still with the Lord.
Then Jesus asked the most important question:
"Do you believe this?"
He did not ask:
How much theology do you know?
He did not ask:
How many meetings do you attend?
He did not ask:
How many good deeds do you do?
He asked only:
"Do you believe this?"
Because what truly changes a life
is not knowing,
but believing.
To this day,
Jesus still places the same question before us:
When sickness comes,
do you believe?
When death comes,
do you believe?
When hope seems shattered,
do you believe?
Finally Martha answered:
"Yes, Lord. I have believed."
This is a beautiful confession of faith.
Although she had not yet seen the miracle;
although Lazarus was still in the tomb;
although the tears had not stopped;
she chose to believe.
True faith
is not believing after we have seen;
it is believing God
before we see.
This passage reminds us:
First, resurrection is not a future event but Jesus Himself. Where Jesus is, there is the hope of resurrection.
Second, the source of life is not in the world but in Christ. Apart from Him, people cannot have true life.
Third, believers will experience death, but death is not the end. Because Christ has overcome death.
Fourth, eternal life begins the moment we believe in Jesus. It is not only a hope after death, but a life we have now.
Fifth, Jesus still asks us today: "Do you believe this?" Faith is not knowing, but believing and entrusting.
q: When you face what you fear most in life, do you still believe that Jesus is the resurrection and the life?
If Jesus asked you today, "Do you believe this?" what would your answer be?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You for showing us through Jesus that He is the resurrection and the life. When we face loss, sickness, and death in life, strengthen our faith. Let us know that life is not in circumstances, but in Christ. Even with a tomb before us, we still believe You have resurrection power. We pray in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, amen.

v: When she had said this, she went away and called Mary, her sister, secretly, saying, “The Teacher is here and is calling you.”
When she heard this, she arose quickly and went to him.
Now Jesus had not yet come into the village, but was in the place where Martha met him.
Then the Jews who were with her in the house and were consoling her, when they saw Mary, that she rose up quickly and went out, followed her, saying, “She is going to the tomb to weep there.”
Therefore when Mary came to where Jesus was and saw him, she fell down at his feet, saying to him, “Lord, if you would have been here, my brother wouldn’t have died.”
b: This passage is full of deep emotion.
If Martha earlier represented faith expressed through reason,
then Mary here
represents faith expressed through emotion.
God accepts not only our reason,
but also our tears.
God understands not only our thoughts,
but also our feelings.
The text begins:
"The Teacher is here, and is calling you."
These words are short,
yet full of warmth.
In Mary's most sorrowful moment,
Jesus had not forgotten her.
The Lord did not come only to see Lazarus' tomb;
the Lord also came looking for a wounded heart.
Many times,
what people fear most in pain is not the problem itself,
but the feeling of being forgotten.
But the gospel tells us:
the Lord knows;
the Lord remembers;
the Lord is looking for you.
Just as when Adam hid in the garden,
God called out:
"Where are you?"
Today,
Jesus is still looking for the brokenhearted.
Verse 29 says:
"When she heard this, she arose quickly, and went to him."
This is a consistent trait of Mary.
She always ran to Jesus.
In Luke chapter ten,
she sat at the Lord's feet listening to His word;
later she poured perfume on the Lord;
now in her sorrow,
she still comes before the Lord.
A truly spiritual person
does not necessarily never weep;
does not necessarily have no weakness;
but he brings his tears to the Lord.
Some, after being hurt, turn away from God;
some, after pain, complain against God;
but Mary chose to draw near to the Lord.
This is one of the most precious expressions of faith.
Then the text says:
"Now Jesus had not yet come into the village."
This is an interesting detail.
Jesus was in no hurry to perform a miracle;
He did not go straight to the tomb;
He first stayed outside the village.
Because to the Lord,
people matter more than events.
Relationship matters more than miracles.
God does not only want to solve problems;
God cares more about the human heart.
Many times,
we just want to fix the circumstances quickly;
but Jesus first wants to heal what is inside us.
Verse 31 mentions
that many people followed Mary,
thinking she was going to the tomb to weep.
Because in their eyes,
