this was the most natural response.
Having lost a loved one,
of course she would go to the tomb.
But they did not know
that Mary was not going first to the tomb,
but first to find Jesus.
This is a very deep spiritual principle:
when life meets death and loss,
do not run first to despair,
but run first to Jesus.
Because a tomb cannot answer questions;
only Jesus can.
Then in verse 32,
Mary came to Jesus.
The text says:
"she fell down at his feet."
This was the position most familiar to Mary.
She had once listened at the Lord's feet;
she had once worshiped at the Lord's feet;
now she also weeps at the Lord's feet.
One who is truly close to the Lord
knows where the safest place is.
Not in people's arms;
not in the world's comfort;
but at the Lord's feet.
Then she said words almost identical to Martha's:
"Lord, if you would have been here, my brother wouldn't have died."
In these words there is faith,
and also pain.
She believed Jesus could heal the sick;
yet she did not understand why Jesus had not come sooner.
She loved the Lord;
yet she still had questions.
This shows us something precious:
true faith
does not mean never having questions.
God never asked us to pretend to be strong.
The Psalms are full of questions;
Jeremiah wept;
Habakkuk asked;
David poured out his heart.
God is not afraid of our coming with tears.
What God fears is that we will not come.
Mary did not hide her disappointment,
but brought it to Jesus.
This is exactly where healing begins.
Many times,
the starting point of a miracle is not power,
but honesty.
When a person is willing to bring his true heart to the Lord,
God's work begins.
This passage reminds us:
First, Jesus does not forget the brokenhearted. In the most painful moments, the Lord still remembers you.
Second, true faith is not the absence of tears but coming to the Lord with tears. Mary chose to run to Jesus.
Third, people matter more than events. God not only solves problems but also cares about our hearts.
Fourth, a tomb cannot give answers; Jesus can. In loss, seek the Lord first.
Fifth, God accepts our real emotions. We may come before Him with questions, weakness, and tears.
q: When you are hurt or disappointed, what do you run to first?
Are you willing to bring your most honest emotions and tears to Jesus?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You that You are a God who understands our tears. When we face loss, pain, and confusion, help us not to turn away from You, but, like Mary, to come to Your feet. Comfort the brokenhearted, heal the crushed spirit, and let us find strength and hope again in Your presence. We pray in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, amen.

v: When Jesus therefore saw her weeping, and the Jews weeping who came with her, he groaned in the spirit, and was troubled,
and said, “Where have you laid him?” They told him, “Lord, come and see.”
Jesus wept.
The Jews therefore said, “See how much affection he had for him!”
Some of them said, “Couldn’t this man, who opened the eyes of him who was blind, have also kept this man from dying?”
b: This passage is the home of the shortest verse in the whole Bible:
"Jesus wept."
Only two words,
yet they hold deep love and comfort.
This Lord who was about to raise the dead
stood weeping beside a tomb.
This Lord who knew that in a few minutes Lazarus would walk out of the tomb
wept all the same.
Why?
Because God is not only an almighty God,
but also a God full of compassion.
The text says:
"When Jesus therefore saw her weeping."
What the Lord saw first
was not the tomb;
not death;
not the miracle;
but people's tears.
This shows us:
God does not look at our pain with indifference.
He sees our tears in the night;
sees the wounds in our hearts;
sees the burdens we cannot tell anyone.
Psalm 56:8 says:
"You keep track of my wanderings. Put my tears into your bottle."
In God's eyes,
every tear has value.
Then the text says:
"he groaned in the spirit, and was troubled."
The original meaning is very strong,
even carrying a sense of agitation and indignation.
Jesus was not merely sad.
He was facing all the destruction that death brings.
When God first created the world,
there was no death.
Death is the result brought by sin entering the world.
So when Jesus stood before the tomb,
what He saw was not only Lazarus' death,
but the tragedy of the whole fallen world.
He saw:
sin bringing separation;
death bringing tears;
darkness bringing pain;
Satan bringing ruin.
So His heart was deeply moved.
This is also why Jesus later went to the cross.
Because He came
to deal with sin and death once for all.
In verse 34,
Jesus asked:
"Where have you laid him?"
Of course,
Jesus was not unaware.
He already knew where the tomb was.
But He wanted people to bring the problem to Him.
Many times,
God also asks us:
Where is your wound?
Where is your pain?
Where is your tomb?
The Lord is not unaware;
He wants us to be willing to bring it to Him.
Then,
John records the shortest verse in all of Scripture:
"Jesus wept."
This is a most precious truth.
God is not a God who sits far above,
unable to understand people.
He once became a man;
He once was hungry;
He once was weary;
He once was rejected;
He once wept.
Therefore,
there is no pain He does not understand.
Hebrews 4:15 says:
"For we don't have a high priest who can't empathize with our weaknesses."
When you weep,
Jesus knows.
When your heart is broken,
Jesus understands.
When you feel alone,
Jesus is with you.
He does not stand at a distance giving instructions,
but walks into our pain.
Verse 36,
the people said:
"See how much he loved him!"
At least they got one thing right.
Jesus' tears
prove His love.
Sometimes,
God's love is not to change our circumstances at once;
but first to walk with us through them.
Sometimes,
the greatest comfort is not an answer,
but presence.
Then in verse 37,
some began to question again:
"Couldn't this man, who opened the eyes of him who was blind, have also kept this man from dying?"
This is really the question of many:
If God has power,
why did He not work sooner?
If God loves me,
why did He allow this to happen?
Yet
they did not know
that Jesus had not come too late;
He was about to reveal a greater glory.
God's timing
often goes beyond human understanding.
People want to avoid death;
God wants to display resurrection.
People want to solve the problem;
God wants to reveal Himself.
This passage reminds us:
First, Jesus sees people's tears. He is not an indifferent God but a compassionate God.
Second, death and pain were not God's original intention. Jesus grieved over the destruction that sin and death bring.
Third, Jesus wept. He fully understands human weakness and sorrow.
Fourth, God's greatest comfort is often His presence. He is willing to walk with us through pain.
Fifth, when we see delay, God is preparing a greater glory. Do not lose faith because of waiting.
q: Do you have hidden tears and wounds lately?
Are you willing to believe that Jesus not only knows, but is walking with you through it?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You that You are a God who weeps. When our hearts are broken, You understand; when we cry, You see. Be our strength in our weakness and our comfort in our sorrow. Help us believe that even when we cannot yet see the answer, You are with us, and You are bringing about a greater glory. We pray in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, amen.

v: Jesus therefore, again groaning in himself, came to the tomb. Now it was a cave, and a stone lay against it.
Jesus said, “Take away the stone.” Martha, the sister of him who was dead, said to him, “Lord, by this time there is a stench, for he has been dead four days.”
Jesus said to her, “Didn’t I tell you that if you believed, you would see God’s glory?”
b: This passage is the key turning point of the miracle of Lazarus' resurrection.
Because the miracle is about to happen.
Yet before the miracle happens,
a stone must first be rolled away.
Many times,
it is not that God's power cannot work,
but that people keep leaving the stone where it is.
The text says:
"Jesus therefore, again groaning in himself."
This is already the second mention.
John repeats it deliberately,
because Jesus was not calmly standing beside the tomb as an observer.
He deeply felt the destruction of death.
He came
to defeat death.
He came
to bring life back to humankind.
And this tomb before Him
symbolized the condition of all humanity held under sin and death.
Then the text says:
"Now it was a cave, and a stone lay against it."
In those days,
tombs were usually cut into rock,
with the entrance sealed by a large stone.
The stone stands for:
the end;
despair;
helplessness;
a limit that people cannot break through.
Today,
many people also have their own stones in life.
It may be:
years of hurt;
someone you cannot forgive;
a long-standing sinful habit;
a broken family;
illness;
failure;
despair.
These stones block the way in front of life,
making people feel there is no hope.
But when Jesus came to the tomb,
the first thing He did was not to call Lazarus out.
It was:
"Take away the stone."
How interesting.
Jesus fully had the power to make the stone roll away Himself.
He had calmed the storm;
He could make the blind see;
He could raise the dead.
Of course He could also move a stone.
Yet He wanted people to take part.
This is a spiritual principle:
God often does the part only God can do,
and asks us to do the part that is ours.
God can raise the dead;
but people must roll away the stone.
God can heal a life;
but people must be willing to open the door of their heart.
God can set people free;
but people must be willing to obey.
Then Martha immediately raised a practical objection:
"Lord, by this time there is a stench."
The meaning in the original is:
the body has already begun to decay.
Martha was really reminding Jesus:
It's too late.
It's too late now.
The matter is beyond the point of recovery.
Aren't we often like this too?
God says to us:
Believe once more.
We say:
It's been too long.
God says:
I can restore.
We say:
It's already broken.
God says:
I can heal.
We say:
There is no hope left.
Martha's problem was not that she did not believe God had power,
but that
she thought this problem had gone beyond the reach of God's work.
Many times,
we believe God can do many things,
yet doubt whether God can handle "this one thing."
So Jesus answered:
"Didn't I tell you that if you believed, you would see God's glory?"
Notice.
Jesus did not say:
Believe after you see.
He said:
Believe first, and then see.
The logic of the world is:
seeing is believing.
The principle of God's kingdom is:
believe, and then you will see.
Faith is not denying reality;
faith is believing God above reality.
Lazarus really was dead;
the body really had begun to decay;
the stone really did block the tomb.
But God's glory is greater than all these.
"Glory" in John's Gospel
does not mean an abstract feeling.
It means:
God's real presence being revealed;
God's power being displayed;
God's identity being seen.
In other words,
Jesus was saying:
Martha,
do not keep looking at the tomb;
look at God.
Do not keep looking at the stone;
look at God.
Do not keep looking at death;
look at the glory of God.
This is also a lesson we need to learn today.
Because many times,
we focus so much on the problem
that we forget God.
We focus so much on circumstances
that we forget the Lord.
We focus so much on the stone
that we forget the risen Lord is right beside us.
This passage reminds us:
First, Jesus came to overcome death and despair. No tomb can limit His power.
Second, God often asks us to roll away the stone first. Obedience is often the beginning of a miracle.
Third, we often feel it is too late, but God is never too late. The end of man is not the end of God.
Fourth, faith is not denying reality but looking to God within reality. Do not see only the tomb; see the Lord too.
Fifth, God's glory is greater than all our problems. When we believe, we will see God's work.
q: What is the biggest "stone" in your life right now?
Are you willing to obey the Lord, roll the stone away, and let God's glory be revealed?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, shine Your light on the stones in our lives that hinder Your work. Help us be willing to obey Your leading and roll away fear, doubt, bitterness, and despair. Give us also real faith, to see not only the problem but Your glory. May we believe that with You it is never too late, for You reign forever. We pray in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, amen.

v: So they took away the stone from the place where the dead man was lying. Jesus lifted up his eyes, and said, “Father, I thank you that you listened to me.
I know that you always listen to me, but because of the multitude standing around I said this, that they may believe that you sent me.”
When he had said this, he cried with a loud voice, “Lazarus, come out!”
He who was dead came out, bound hand and foot with wrappings, and his face was wrapped around with a cloth. Jesus said to them, “Free him, and let him go.”
b: This is one of the most stirring miracles in John's Gospel.
A man who had been dead four days
walked out of the tomb.
This was not just healing;
not improvement;
not recovery of health;
but:
life overcoming death.
This miracle foretold something even greater—
Jesus Himself would rise from the dead.
The text begins:
"So they took away the stone."
This sentence seems simple,
yet it is the important starting point of the miracle.
Earlier Jesus commanded people to roll away the stone,
and now they finally obeyed.
Notice,
the miracle did not happen before the stone was moved,
but after the stone was moved.
Many times,
we keep waiting for God to work;
but God is waiting for us to obey.
God has already prepared the power;
but people are still clinging to the stone they will not let go of.
When obedience appears,
God's power begins to move.
Then Jesus lifted up His eyes to heaven.
He did not first walk to the tomb;
He did not first cry out loudly;
but first prayed to the Father.
This shows us:
all of Jesus' power
is built on His relationship with the Father.
He never acted independently.
He lived a life of complete dependence on the Heavenly Father.
This is also the example the Lord gives us.
Truly powerful people
are often also those who know best how to depend on God.
Then Jesus said:
"Father, I thank you that you listened to me."
How interesting.
Lazarus had not yet come out,
the miracle had not yet happened,
yet Jesus gave thanks first.
This is the expression of real faith.
Many people
thank only after they have seen.
Jesus
believed the Father had already accomplished it, so He gave thanks first.
Thanksgiving is not the result,
but faith.
Then Jesus said:
"because of the multitude standing around I said this."
Jesus was not doubting whether the Father had heard.
He knew the Father always hears Him.
He prayed this way
so that the crowd would understand:
He was sent by the Father.
The greatest purpose of the whole miracle
was not to amaze people,
but to lead people to believe.
The miracle itself is not the destination;
knowing Jesus is the destination.
Then comes the most striking scene of the whole passage.
Jesus cried with a loud voice:
"Lazarus, come out!"
Just a few words,
yet they shook the power of death.
Augustine once said:
if Jesus had not called "Lazarus" by name,
everyone in the tombs might have come out.
Because at the voice of the Lord of life,
even death must obey.
In Genesis,
God said:
"Let there be light."
And there was light.
Now,
the Son of God says:
"Lazarus, come out!"
And the dead man came out.
Because in His word is the power to create life.
This is also the power of the gospel.
Every person who is saved
has in fact experienced a spiritual Lazarus miracle.
Ephesians 2 says:
we were once dead in trespasses and sins.
It was Christ who called us out.
Those who were dead in sin,
by the Lord's call,
received new life.
Then the text says:
"He who was dead came out."
John wrote it very simply.
No exaggerated description;
no sensational coloring.
He just calmly records:
the dead man came out.
Because before the Lord of life,
death is not a problem.
Yet when Lazarus came out,
there was still one more situation:
"bound hand and foot with wrappings, and his face was wrapped around with a cloth."
He was alive,
yet still wrapped up.
This is a very deep spiritual picture.
Many Christians are already saved;
they already have life;
yet they are still limited by some old bindings.
For example:
past hurts;
wrong thinking;
fear;
bitterness;
sinful habits;
low self-esteem;
pride.
So Jesus said:
"Free him, and let him go!"
God does not only want people to come alive,
He also wants people to be free.
Salvation is only the beginning;
the release and renewal of life still need to continue.
This is also an important mission of the church in serving one another.
To help people shed their wrappings
and live out the freedom of God's children.
This passage reminds us:
First, obedience is often the beginning of a miracle. Only after the stone is moved is God's power revealed.
Second, true power comes from an intimate relationship with the Father. Jesus prayed first, then did the miracle.
Third, Jesus' words carry the power of life. When He calls, death retreats.
Fourth, everyone who is saved experiences a spiritual resurrection. The Lord called us out of sin.
Fifth, God wants us not only to come alive but also to be free. The renewal of life is a continuing process throughout our lives.
q: Are there still some "grave clothes" in your life that are entangling you?
Are you willing to let Jesus give you not only life, but also bring you into true freedom?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You for showing us resurrection power through Jesus. When there is death, despair, and darkness in our lives, say to us again, "Come out!" Set us free from sin, fear, and bondage. Help us also to shed everything that entangles us and live out the free and abundant new life You have given. We pray in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, amen.

v: Therefore many of the Jews who came to Mary and saw what Jesus did believed in him.
But some of them went away to the Pharisees and told them the things which Jesus had done.
The chief priests therefore and the Pharisees gathered a council, and said, “What are we doing? For this man does many signs.
If we leave him alone like this, everyone will believe in him, and the Romans will come and take away both our place and our nation.”
b: Lazarus was raised.
The dead man walked out of the tomb.
This is one of the greatest miracles in John's Gospel.
By human thinking,
everyone who saw it should have believed in Jesus.
Yet the text shows us a startling fact:
the same miracle led some to trust the Lord, and others to reject Him all the more.
The problem is not the miracle,
but the human heart.
Verse 45 says:
"Many believed in him."
This is the original purpose of the miracle.
God's work is not meant to satisfy people's curiosity,
but to lead people to know Jesus.
When these people saw the dead raised,
they finally understood:
this was no ordinary teacher;
not a prophet;
not a religious figure;
but the Christ sent by God.
So they believed.
A truly tender heart,
seeing God's work,
draws nearer to God.
Yet verse 46 immediately brings in another group:
"But some of them went away to the Pharisees."
They saw the same miracle,
yet were not moved.
Instead they ran to report to the religious leaders.
This again proves that
those who do not believe
do not lack evidence;
they are unwilling to accept the evidence.
Many people think:
If I saw a miracle with my own eyes, I would surely believe.
Actually, not necessarily.
Because the greatest problem of faith
is often not the eyes,
but the heart.
The Israelites saw the Red Sea part;
saw manna fall from heaven;
saw the pillar of cloud and fire;
yet still complained.
The Pharisees saw the blind healed;
saw the dead raised;
yet still rejected Jesus.
A miracle by itself cannot change a hardened heart.
Only those willing to surrender
can truly know God.
Then in verse 47,
the chief priests and Pharisees called a council.
This was the highest religious council of the Jews.
They said:
"What are we doing? For this man does many signs."
Notice,
they did not deny the miracles.
They admitted:
Jesus had indeed done many signs.
The question was not:
"Did He perform miracles?"
but:
"What shall we do?"
Here the darkness of human nature is revealed.
When truth threatens people's interests,
people often do not seek the truth,
but seek to protect themselves.
Then verse 48 reveals their real worry:
"If we leave him alone like this, everyone will believe in him."
On the surface it looks like concern for the nation,
but actually it is concern for themselves.
Because if everyone follows Jesus,
what becomes of their authority?
What becomes of their position?
What becomes of their influence?
Many times,
what keeps people from believing in the Lord
is not a question of reason,
but a question of lordship.
The greatest struggle of man is not:
"Does God exist?"
but:
"Who is King?"
The Pharisees' problem
was exactly this.
They were afraid of losing control.
So they said:
"the Romans will come and take away both our place and our nation."
This is typical fear-driven thinking.
They thought:
if we accept Jesus,
we will lose everything.
Yet history proves
that after they rejected Jesus,
the Roman army still destroyed Jerusalem and the temple in AD 70.
What they tried to hold on to
was lost in the end anyway.
This is a deep spiritual principle:
whoever tries to hold on to his own life will lose it in the end; whoever is willing to hand it over to God will gain it instead.
Jesus later said:
"For whoever wants to save his life will lose it, and whoever will lose his life for my sake will find it."
The Pharisees chose to protect themselves,
and lost true life.
This passage reminds us:
First, seeing the same work of God, different people respond differently. The key is not evidence but the heart.
Second, a hardened heart may reject God even after seeing a miracle. Faith requires humility.
Third, our greatest problem is often not that we do not know the truth but that we are unwilling to accept it. Because truth challenges our lordship.
Fourth, fear leads people to wrong decisions. When we only want to protect ourselves, we easily drift from God.
Fifth, true security is not in power, position, and control, but in God. Only those who entrust themselves to the Lord find true life.
q: Is there something in your life you are afraid of losing that is keeping you from following the Lord more deeply?
When God challenges your lordship, will you choose to believe, or hold on to yourself?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, guard our hearts from rejecting You, as the Pharisees did, out of pride and fear. Give us a tender, teachable spirit, so that when we see Your work we are willing to surrender and believe. Help us also to let go of our grip on control and place the lordship of our lives in Your hands, for You alone are the true King. We pray in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, amen.

v: But a certain one of them, Caiaphas, being high priest that year, said to them, “You know nothing at all,
nor do you consider that it is advantageous for us that one man should die for the people, and that the whole nation not perish.”
Now he didn’t say this of himself, but being high priest that year, he prophesied that Jesus would die for the nation,
and not for the nation only, but that he might also gather together into one the children of God who are scattered abroad.
b: This passage is one of the most ironic in John's Gospel.
Because the one who spoke the core truth of the gospel
was a high priest who opposed Jesus.
This shows us:
God can even use those who oppose Him to accomplish His purpose.
Caiaphas in the text
was the high priest of the Jews at that time.
His intention was not to worship God,
but to get rid of Jesus.
Yet
God, through his mouth,
spoke the very heart of the message of salvation.
In verse 49,
Caiaphas impatiently said:
"You know nothing at all."
He thought himself wiser than the others.
This was the thinking of a politician.
In his eyes,
Jesus was not a Savior,
but a troublemaker.
If He were removed,
the problem would be solved.
So he put forward his plan:
"it is advantageous for you that one man should die for the people, and that the whole nation not perish."
From a political point of view,
he meant:
sacrifice one man, Jesus,
to preserve the whole nation.
This was a realist's calculation.
Yet
he did not know he was speaking God's eternal plan.
Because Jesus really would die for the people.
Only the meaning was completely different.
What Caiaphas thought of was a political sacrifice;
what God accomplished was atonement for salvation.
What Caiaphas thought of was saving a nation;
God wanted to save all humankind.
So John immediately explains:
"Now he didn't say this of himself."
This does not mean Caiaphas was devout.
It means that God goes beyond human intentions
and rules over history.
Just like Balaam in the Old Testament, who meant to curse Israel,
yet God made his mouth speak blessing.
God is always higher than human plans.
This also gives us great comfort.
Today the world seems chaotic;
hearts are full of calculation;
politics is full of struggle;
circumstances are full of uncertainty.
But God still reigns.
No one can ruin God's final purpose.
Then John says:
"Jesus was about to die for the nation."
This "for"
is the very core of the gospel.
Jesus did not die by accident;
did not die in failure;
did not die because He was powerless to resist.
He died
in our place.
Isaiah 53 had long since prophesied:
"he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities."
The greatest meaning of the cross
is substitution.
It was we who should have died;
it was we who should have been judged;
it was we who should have borne the price of sin.
Yet Jesus took our place.
This is grace.
Grace is not God overlooking sin;
but God Himself bearing sin.
Then in verse 52,
John widens the view:
"and not for the nation only."
Jesus did not die only for the Jews.
He came for the whole world.
This fulfills God's promise to Abraham:
"in you all the families of the earth will be blessed."
From Genesis on,
God's plan was never only to save one nation,
but to save all peoples.
So the gospel has no racial boundary;
no cultural boundary;
no class boundary.
Whoever is willing to believe
can receive salvation.
Finally John says:
"that he might also gather together into one the children of God who are scattered abroad."
Sin brings division.
People divided from God;
people divided from people;
nation from nation;
family from family.
But the cross brings unity.
Because in Christ,
all who believe become one family.
True unity
is not by institutions;
not by politics;
not by human effort to maintain it.
True unity
comes because we share one Savior.
This is also a picture of God's kingdom.
From every tribe, people, region, and nation,
gathered together by the Lord,
worshiping the Lamb together.
This passage reminds us:
First, God can use anyone to accomplish His purpose. Even those who oppose Him cannot hinder Him.
Second, Jesus' death was no accident but God's eternal plan of salvation. The cross was already in God's preparation.
Third, the heart of the gospel is substitution. Jesus bore the punishment of sin in our place.
Fourth, Jesus died not only for the Jews but for the whole world. Salvation is open to all.
Fifth, the cross brings true unity. All who belong to the Lord become one family in Christ.
q: Do you truly understand the meaning of "Jesus died for me"?
How can you live out a thankful response to the grace of the cross today?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You for sending Jesus into the world to bear the punishment of our sin in our place. Thank You for revealing, at the cross, how wide and long and high and deep is Your love. Let us not only know salvation but often give thanks for the grace of Your atonement. Teach us also, in Christ, to love one another and accept one another, and to live out the unity of God's family. We pray in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, amen.

v: So from that day forward they took counsel that they might put him to death.
Jesus therefore walked no more openly among the Jews, but departed from there into the country near the wilderness, to a city called Ephraim. He stayed there with his disciples.
Now the Passover of the Jews was at hand. Many went up from the country to Jerusalem before the Passover, to purify themselves.
Then they sought for Jesus and spoke with one another as they stood in the temple, “What do you think—that he isn’t coming to the feast at all?”
Now the chief priests and the Pharisees had commanded that if anyone knew where he was, he should report it, that they might seize him.
b: This passage is an important turning point in John's Gospel.
After Lazarus was raised,
Jesus' fame reached its peak;
and at the same time,
the opposition against Him reached its peak.
From here on,
the footsteps toward the cross draw ever nearer.
Verse 53 says:
"So from that day on they took counsel that they might put him to death."
Notice,
this was not a momentary impulse.
Not an emotional reaction.
But a formal resolution.
The religious leaders had made up their minds:
Jesus must die.
This is deeply ironic.
Jesus healed the sick;
fed the crowds;
comforted the grieving;
raised the dead;
everything He did was good.
Yet
people wanted to kill Him.
This again shows:
the problem was never that Jesus had done something wrong.
The problem was:
the light shone into the darkness,
but the darkness was unwilling to receive the light.
John chapter 1 had already said:
"The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness hasn't overcome it."
It is the same today.
Sometimes,
when truth touches people's pride;
when the gospel challenges people's lordship;
when God calls people to repent;
people may choose to refuse.
Not because the truth is unclear,
but because they are unwilling to surrender.
Then verse 54 says:
"Jesus therefore walked no more openly among the Jews."
This was not because Jesus was afraid.
The whole Gospel of John tells us again and again:
His hour had not yet come.
Jesus' life
was lived entirely within the Father's timetable.
He did not move ahead of time;
nor did He delay.
This is an important spiritual lesson.
Many times,
we either run too fast
or stop too long.
But Jesus lived in God's rhythm.
He knew when to move forward;
when to stay;
when to be public;
when to be hidden.
A truly mature life
does not act on impulse,
but follows God's timing.
Then John mentions:
"Now the Passover of the Jews was at hand."
This sentence seems ordinary,
yet it is full of meaning.
Because the Passover commemorates:
the lamb's blood shed;
Israel being saved;
death passing over them.
And now,
the true Passover Lamb was about to arrive.
The lamb in Egypt
could save only for a night.
But Jesus, the Lamb of God,
would save the world from sin.
From the very beginning of John's Gospel,
John the Baptist declared:
"Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!"
Now,
the Lamb was about to walk to the altar.
Then verse 55 says:
"many went up to Jerusalem out of the country before the Passover, to purify themselves."
Everyone was preparing for the feast.
They washed their bodies;
kept the rituals;
prepared to worship.
But the irony is,
they were seeking religious purification
while the Lord who could truly cleanse sin was among them.
Many times,
people are busy with religious activity
yet neglect a real relationship with God.
Outwardly they may be very pious,
yet inwardly far from God.
Therefore,
what God cares about most is not ritual,
but the heart.
Verse 56 says:
"Then they sought for Jesus."
There are two different kinds of seeking here.
Some were seeking a Savior;
some were seeking a target so they could seize Him.
Both were seeking Jesus,
yet their motives were completely different.
It is the same to this day.
Some come to church to know the Lord;
some come only seeking blessings;
some come to fulfill a religious duty;
some truly long for God.
What God values
is not only whether we seek Him,
but why we seek Him.
Finally verse 57:
"if anyone knew where he was, he should report it."
The religious leaders wanted to seize Jesus.
But they did not know
that the ones really in control were not them.
On the surface,
they were making plans;
in reality God was reigning.
On the surface,
Jesus was about to be arrested;
in reality He was willingly walking to the cross.
It was not that people took His life;
He gladly laid it down.
The cross is not failure;
it is the victory of salvation.
This passage reminds us:
First, when the light shines into darkness, people must choose. Receive the light, or reject it.
Second, Jesus always lived within the Father's timetable. A mature life learns to follow God's rhythm.
Third, the Passover points to Christ. Jesus is the true Lamb who takes away the sin of the world.
Fourth, religious activity cannot replace a relationship with God. What God values is the heart.
Fifth, God always reigns. Even when circumstances seem chaotic, His plan never fails.
q: Are you willing to live by God's timing, rather than your own?
Do you seek Jesus for what you can get, or because you truly long for Him?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You for reigning over history and over our lives. When we see chaotic circumstances and darkened hearts, help us still believe that Your plan has not changed. Keep us also from stopping at religious form, and help us truly seek You and follow You. May we walk in Your light all our lives and live in Your timing. We pray in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, amen.

v: Then six days before the Passover, Jesus came to Bethany, where Lazarus was, who had been dead, whom he raised from the dead.
So they made him a supper there. Martha served, but Lazarus was one of those who sat at the table with him.
Therefore Mary took a pound of ointment of pure nard, very precious, and anointed Jesus’s feet and wiped his feet with her hair. The house was filled with the fragrance of the ointment.
b: John chapter twelve is the beginning of the last week before Jesus' suffering.
In a few more days,
He would ride a donkey into Jerusalem;
in a few more days,
He would be betrayed;
in a few more days,
He would go to the cross.
At just this moment,
a most beautiful picture appears in Bethany.
Someone serves;
someone bears witness;
someone worships.
And the one who shines brightest among them
is Mary.
Verse 1 says:
"Jesus came to Bethany."
This is a place full of memories.
Not long before,
Lazarus had lain in the tomb.
Death had shrouded this family.
Tears had filled this village.
But now,
Lazarus sits alive at the table.
This reminds us:
God can change the story of a life.
Yesterday's tomb
can become today's testimony.
Yesterday's tears
can become today's thanksgiving.
Yesterday's despair
can become today's praise.
This is the power of the gospel.
Verse 2 mentions three people.
First:
"Martha served."
Martha was still serving.
Interestingly,
Scripture does not say that she changed her personality.
She was still busy;
still serving.
But this time,
there was no complaining;
no comparing;
no resenting her sister.
Because after the earlier experiences,
her life seemed to have matured.
True service
is not out of pressure;
but out of love.
Not to prove oneself;
but to glorify the Lord.
Next:
"Lazarus was one of those sitting at the table with him."
What a wonderful sentence.
In the previous chapter,
he was still in the tomb.
Now,
he sits at the Lord's table.
This itself is a testimony.
He did not preach;
did not give a testimony;
did not do anything great.
He just sat there.
But when people saw him,
they knew:
Jesus is real.
Sometimes,
a life itself is the most powerful testimony.
A person changed by the Lord
does not need to say much.
His life
is a living testimony.
Then,
the focus turns to Mary.
Verse 3 says:
"Mary took a pound of ointment of pure nard, very precious."
This perfume came from India
and was extremely expensive.
According to the account that follows,
it was worth about three hundred denarii,
about a working man's wages for a year.
This may have been Mary's most precious possession.
Yet
she gave it to Jesus without holding anything back.
This is love.
True love
is always willing to pay a price.
David once said:
"I won't offer burnt offerings to Yahweh my God which cost me nothing."
An offering that costs nothing
often has no depth.
One who has truly experienced the Lord's grace
will gladly give the best to the Lord.
Then the text says:
"anointed the feet of Jesus."
In that culture,
the feet were the lowest part of the body.
Mary chose to kneel at the lowest place.
True worship
is not exalting oneself;
but exalting Christ.
One who truly knows Jesus
grows more and more humble.
Because the more we know the Lord's glory,
the more we see our own limits.
Then the text says:
"and wiped his feet with her hair."
In Jewish culture,
a woman's hair was regarded as her glory.
Mary laid her own glory at the Lord's feet.
This is a very deep spiritual picture.
True worship
is giving our own glory to the Lord.
Giving the lordship to the Lord;
giving the future to the Lord;
giving the most precious to the Lord.
This is exactly the core that the 321 principles emphasize:
let Jesus be King;
let Jesus receive all the glory.
Finally John writes a very beautiful sentence:
"the house was filled with the fragrance of the ointment."
When Mary worshiped the Lord,
the fragrance filled the whole house.
Worship is never just a personal matter.
One who truly loves the Lord
will influence those around him.
One whose life carries the fragrance of Christ
will affect the whole environment.
Paul later said:
"For we are to God a sweet aroma of Christ, in those who are saved and in those who perish."
Those who truly love the Lord
give off a heavenly fragrance in their lives.
This fragrance is not perfume,
but the life of Christ.
This passage reminds us:
First, God can turn a tomb into a testimony. Yesterday's despair can become today's glory.
Second, mature service comes from love, not pressure. Martha served the Lord quietly.
Third, a changed life is itself the most powerful testimony. Lazarus sitting there was a testimony.
Fourth, true love is always willing to pay a price. Mary gave the most precious thing to Jesus.
Fifth, true worship gives off the fragrance of Christ. When we exalt the Lord, those around us also sense the Lord's presence.
q: What is the most precious thing in your life? Are you willing to give it to the Lord?
Can others smell the fragrance of Christ through your life?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You for bringing us from death into life, from despair into hope. Give us a heart that loves the Lord like Mary, willing to give You our best and lay our own glory at Your feet. Make our lives give off the fragrance of Christ, so that those around us see Your beauty through us. We pray in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, amen.

v: Then Judas Iscariot, Simon’s son, one of his disciples, who would betray him, said,
“Why wasn’t this ointment sold for three hundred denarii, and given to the poor?”
Now he said this, not because he cared for the poor, but because he was a thief, and having the money box, used to steal what was put into it.
But Jesus said, “Leave her alone. She has kept this for the day of my burial.
For you always have the poor with you, but you don’t always have me.”
b: At the feast in Bethany,
when Mary offered the most precious perfume to Jesus,
the whole room was filled with fragrance.
Yet
not everyone was moved.
One man saw the same scene,
and his heart was full of criticism.
That man was Judas.
This passage shows us:
people who come close to Jesus in the same way may have completely different lives.
Mary loved the Lord more and more;
Judas walked, step by step, toward betrayal.
Verse 4 specially introduces him:
"Judas Iscariot, one of his disciples, who would betray him."
When John wrote his Gospel,
these events had already happened.
So he describes Judas by the outcome that came later.
This is a figure who stirs regret.
He followed Jesus for more than three years;
heard the best preaching;
saw the most miracles;
witnessed with his own eyes the dead being raised;
and even became one of the twelve apostles.
Yet
being near Jesus
is not the same as belonging to Jesus.
Sitting in church
is not the same as having one's life governed by the Lord.
What truly determines the direction of a life
is not distance,
but the heart.
Then Judas said:
"Why wasn't this ointment sold for three hundred denarii, and given to the poor?"
At first hearing,
this seems very loving.
It even sounds more spiritual than Mary.
Because helping the poor is of course a good thing.
Yet
John immediately exposes the truth:
"Now he said this, not because he cared for the poor."
So it turns out
this was only a disguise.
Many times,
people's words sound very spiritual,
yet their motives may not be.
God looks not only at actions,
but at the heart.
Man looks at the outward appearance;
God looks at the heart.
Then John says plainly:
"but because he was a thief."
This is a very severe description.
Judas was in charge of the finances,
yet used his position to steal money.
On the surface a disciple;
inwardly controlled by greed.
Notice,
Judas' biggest problem was not money,
but:
greed.
Paul says in 1 Timothy:
"the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil."
Money itself is not the problem;
being controlled by money is the problem.
If a person's master is not Jesus,
something else will be king.
Some are ruled by money;
some are ruled by reputation;
some are ruled by power;
some are ruled by self.
And Judas
was ruled by greed.
So,
when Mary offered the perfume,
what she saw was the Lord's worth;
what Judas saw was the perfume's price.
Those who love the Lord see worth;
those who love the world see only price.
These are two completely different views of life.
Then Jesus said:
"Leave her alone!"
These were protective words.
The Lord spoke up for Mary.
When others misunderstood her,
the Lord knew her heart.
This brings us great comfort.
Many times,
people do not necessarily understand our love for the Lord;
they may even criticize our giving and our devotion.
But what matters is not that everyone understands,
but that the Lord knows.
The Lord sees every tear;
every offering;
every act of faithfulness;
every quiet sacrifice.
The Lord remembers them all.
Then Jesus said:
"She has kept this for the day of my burial."
Very likely Mary herself did not fully understand.
But she was more perceptive than the disciples.
While the other disciples were still arguing over who was greatest,
Mary seemed to have already sensed:
the Lord was about to leave.
Her love
brought her closer to the Lord's heart.
True worship
is not only singing hymns;
it is understanding the Lord's heart.
The more one loves the Lord,
the more one can sense the Lord's intentions.
Finally Jesus said:
"For you always have the poor with you, but you don't always have me."
Jesus was not looking down on the poor.
All His life He cared for the poor.
What He meant was:
at this moment, something more important was happening.
Because He was about to go to the cross.
Some opportunities,
once missed, never come again.
Mary seized this moment.
She gave her best to the Lord.
Many times,
we always think we will love the Lord later;
give later;
serve later;
obey later.
But life carries no guarantee.
Today
is the best time to love the Lord.
Now
is the time to respond to the Lord.
This passage reminds us:
First, being near Jesus does not mean truly belonging to Jesus. What matters is whether the heart lets the Lord be King.
Second, God values motive over appearance. Spiritual words do not necessarily mean a spiritual life.
Third, greed leads people away from God. When something else is king, Jesus no longer comes first.
Fourth, the Lord knows everyone who truly loves Him. Even when misunderstood, the Lord still understands.
Fifth, seize today to love the Lord. Do not leave obedience and giving for the future.
This passage also makes us reflect on the core of the 321 principles:
let Jesus be King.
Mary let Jesus be King,
so she was willing to offer the most precious thing.
Judas let money be king,
so in the end he lost his life.
The greatest problem of life
is never how much we have,
but:
who sits on the throne of our life.
q: What in your life is most likely to take Jesus' place right now?
If Jesus is the most precious Lord of your life, how can you express your love for Him concretely today?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, search our hearts. Do not let us be like Judas, following the Lord outwardly while inwardly controlled by other things. Give us a heart that loves the Lord like Mary, willing to give You what is most precious. May Jesus truly be King and reign in our lives, so that we live for You alone all our days. We pray in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, amen.

v: A large crowd therefore of the Jews learned that he was there, and they came, not for Jesus’ sake only, but that they might see Lazarus also, whom he had raised from the dead.
But the chief priests conspired to put Lazarus to death also,
because on account of him many of the Jews went away and believed in Jesus.
b: Although this passage has only three short verses,
it shows us an important truth:
a person changed by Jesus is himself the most powerful testimony.
Lazarus did not preach;
wrote no theological papers;
gave no public speeches;
Scripture does not even record a single word he said.
Yet many people believed in Jesus because of him.
Because his very existence
was a miracle.
Verse 9 says:
"A large crowd therefore of the Jews learned that he was there, and they came."
These people came to Bethany
with two purposes.
The first was to see Jesus.
The second was to see Lazarus.
Because Lazarus had become a sensation across the whole region.
Everyone knew:
this man had been dead four days;
buried;
and now was alive.
It was an undeniable fact.
People might question theology;
might debate doctrine;
might attack Jesus;
but it was hard to deny the living Lazarus before their eyes.
This brings one thing to mind:
many people are unwilling to read the Bible,
but are willing to read the lives of Christians.
For many seekers the first "Bible" they read
is in fact a Christian.
Through us they come to:
know Christ;
know the gospel;
know God's love.
Therefore,
the testimony of a life is often more powerful than words.
As someone has said:
"The gospel you live
is more convincing than the gospel you speak."
Then verse 10 brings a shocking scene:
"But the chief priests conspired to put Lazarus to death also."
How absurd.
Not only did they want to kill Jesus;
now they wanted to kill Lazarus too.
Why?
Because they could not deny the miracle.
Since they could not deny it,
they simply decided to eliminate the witness.
This reveals how hard the human heart can be.
When people refuse to accept the truth,
they may even choose to destroy the evidence.
Much persecution in history has been like this.
Not because the gospel lacks power,
but because the gospel has too much power.
The brighter the light,
the more uncomfortable the darkness.
So Jesus once said:
"men loved the darkness rather than the light, for their works were evil."
Lazarus being alive
proved that Jesus was real.
Therefore,
he became a threat in the eyes of the religious leaders.
Verse 11 reveals the real reason:
"because on account of him many of the Jews went away and believed in Jesus."
Notice,
what they feared most was not Lazarus.
What they feared was:
people beginning to believe in Jesus.
Lazarus was not the focus;
Jesus was the focus.
A true testimony never exalts oneself,
but leads people to Christ.
John the Baptist was like this;
Lazarus was like this;
Christians today should be like this too.
A truly successful testimony
is not one that makes people say:
"You are amazing."
but one that makes people say:
"Your Lord is great."
Many people think a testimony must be spectacular.
Not necessarily.
Lazarus simply lived.
But the way he lived
said everything.
It is the same today.
When a hot-tempered person becomes gentle;
a selfish person learns to give;
a hopeless person is filled with hope;
a bitter person chooses to forgive;
a person bound by sin finds freedom;
these are all Lazarus-style testimonies.
People may not understand theology,
yet they can read a life.
People may not understand how to interpret Scripture,
yet they can see change.
And a changed life
is the most powerful evidence of the gospel.
This passage reminds us:
First, a person changed by the Lord is himself a testimony. A changed life is more powerful than words.
Second, a true testimony leads people to Jesus. The focus is never ourselves, but Christ.
Third, the power of the gospel often stirs up opposition. When light shines on darkness, darkness naturally resists.
Fourth, people can deny doctrine but find it hard to deny a changed life. The strongest evidence of the gospel is a renewed life.
Fifth, each of us can become a Lazarus. Let others see the power of the risen Lord through us.
This also makes us think:
Lazarus was once dead,
and now lives.
And Paul says:
we too were once dead in trespasses and sins,
and now are made alive in Christ.
Therefore,
every person who is born again and saved
is in fact another Lazarus,
a witness to God's grace.
q: In what areas of your life has Jesus already brought change?
Can others see the power and grace of the risen Lord through you?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You for making us alive from spiritual death. Let our lives be a testimony to the gospel, not only by speaking with our mouths but by living out Christ with our lives. May people see us, not to exalt ourselves, but to see the glory and power of Jesus. May more people, through our lives, be willing to come to know You. We pray in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, amen.

v: On the next day a great multitude had come to the feast. When they heard that Jesus was coming to Jerusalem,
they took the branches of the palm trees and went out to meet him, and cried out, “Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, the King of Israel!”
Jesus, having found a young donkey, sat on it. As it is written,
“Don’t be afraid, daughter of Zion. Behold, your King comes, sitting on a donkey’s colt.”
His disciples didn’t understand these things at first, but when Jesus was glorified, then they remembered that these things were written about him, and that they had done these things to him.
b: This passage records the famous "triumphal entry."
This was the last time Jesus entered Jerusalem in His public ministry.
On the surface,
it looked like a grand welcome;
in fact,
it was the beginning of a King's walk to the cross.
The crowd thought He was about to take the throne,
but Jesus knew
He was heading to the cross.
People hoped for political revival,
but Jesus came to bring spiritual salvation.
Verse 12 says:
"A great multitude had come to the feast."
It was the eve of the Passover.
Jews from all over had gathered in Jerusalem.
The number may have exceeded several hundred thousand.
So when Jesus entered the city,
He at once became the focus of the whole city.
Everyone was talking about:
the raising of Lazarus;
Jesus' miracles;
this mysterious Nazarene.
So the crowds poured out of the city to meet Him.
Verse 13 says:
"took the branches of the palm trees, and went out to meet him."
Palm branches at that time symbolized:
victory;
triumph;
national liberation.
In other words,
the crowd was welcoming Jesus the way one welcomes a king.
They shouted:
"Hosanna!"
Originally it meant:
"Save us!"
Later it gradually became a word of acclaim and praise.
They also shouted:
"Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, the King of Israel!"
They were not wrong.
Jesus really is King.
The problem was:
the king they expected,
and the king Jesus truly came to be,
were not the same.
They expected:
the overthrow of Rome;
the restoration of the nation;
political victory.
Jesus came instead to:
save sinners;
establish God's kingdom;
accomplish salvation.
Many are willing to accept the Jesus they expect,
but not necessarily the real Jesus.
It is the same today.
Some want Jesus to be:
a problem solver;
a wealth provider;
a healer of sickness;
a life counselor.
But they are unwilling to let Him be King.
Yet Jesus did not come to fit people's expectations,
but to fulfill the Father's will.
Then in verse 14,
Jesus did something very special:
"found a young donkey, and sat on it."
When ancient kings rode a war horse,
it meant war.
When they rode a young donkey,
it meant peace.
Jesus did not enter the city on a tall war horse,
but on a humble young donkey.
Because He did not come to start a revolution,
but to bring peace.
Not to conquer Rome,
but to conquer sin.
Not to defeat an enemy army,
but to defeat death.
This also fulfilled the prophecy of Zechariah:
"your King comes, sitting on a donkey's colt."
God's plan never errs.
A prophecy from hundreds of years earlier
was now fully fulfilled.
Verse 15 says:
"Don't be afraid."
This is a message that appears again and again in Scripture.
Because when the King comes,
the people need not fear.
True peace
is not the absence of storms;
but the King reigning.
When Jesus is King,
the heart has peace.
When we make ourselves king,
the heart is full of worry.
Much of people's anxiety
actually comes from wanting to control everything.
But life was never in our hands.
True peace
comes from believing:
the Lord is still seated on the throne.
Verse 16 is an interesting sentence:
"His disciples didn't understand these things at first."
While things were happening,
the disciples could not make sense of them.
Only after Jesus was risen and ascended
did they suddenly understand.
This is also our common experience.
Many times,
God is at work,
and we cannot understand.
We ask:
Why is this happening?
Why does God allow this?
Why is the road so winding?
But looking back years later,
we discover:
God had been leading all along.
God had prepared it long before.
Every step was within His plan.
This passage reminds us:
First, Jesus is the true King. He is not a political leader, but the King of kings.
Second, people often accept the Jesus they expect rather than the real Jesus. Faith means obeying God, not demanding that God fit us.
Third, Jesus riding a young donkey into the city shows He is the King of peace. He came not to conquer people but to save them.
Fourth, when Jesus is King, the heart has true peace. Do not be afraid, for the King has come.
Fifth, God's works sometimes cannot be understood at the time but will be afterward. God's plan always sees farther than we do.
This passage also makes us think about the core of the 321 principles:
let Jesus be King.
The people of Jerusalem welcomed Jesus as King,
but wanted Him to be only a political king.
Today,
Jesus also comes to the door of our lives.
The question is not:
whether He is King.
but:
whether we are willing to let Him be King.
True peace
is not found in circumstances changing,
but in the Lord reigning.
q: What kind of king do you want Jesus to be in your heart?
Have you truly handed the lordship of your life to Him, letting Him reign as King within you?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You for sending Jesus, the King of peace, into the world. Help us not just welcome You with our lips, but truly hand the lordship of our lives to You. When we face the unknown and worry, let us remember: You are still seated on the throne. May Jesus reign as King in our lives, so that we live in Your peace and leading. We pray in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, amen.

v: The multitude therefore that was with him when he called Lazarus out of the tomb and raised him from the dead was testifying about it.
For this cause also the multitude went and met him, because they heard that he had done this sign.
The Pharisees therefore said among themselves, “See how you accomplish nothing. Behold, the world has gone after him.”
b: This passage shows us two completely different reactions.
One group believed because of God's work;
another group became even more hostile because of God's work.
They saw the same miracle,
yet the results were completely different.
Because what truly determines the direction of a person's life
is not what he sees,
but the heart within.
Verse 17 says:
"The multitude therefore that was with him bore witness."
After Lazarus was raised,
many began to spread the news.
They had seen with their own eyes:
a dead man walking out of the tomb;
death overcome by the Lord;
God's power displayed.
So
they could not help but bear witness.
Those who have truly met the Lord
find it hard to stay completely silent.
Because the grace is so real,
the change so profound.
The apostle John later said:
"we cannot help telling what we have seen and heard."
The gospel was never a theory,
but an experience of life.
A person who has truly experienced the Lord,
even if he is not eloquent,
will naturally show a testimony in his life.
Verse 18 says:
"For this cause also the multitude went and met him, because they heard that he had done this sign."
Notice,
these people came because of the testimony.
Some saw the miracle;
some heard the testimony;
and so more people came to know Jesus.
This is exactly how the gospel spreads.
One person bears witness;
another believes;
and goes on to influence more.
God's kingdom often expands just this way.
Not beginning with a grand strategy,
but with one person willing to bear witness.
The Samaritan woman was like this;
the blind man who was healed was like this;
Lazarus was like this too.
So,
do not underestimate your testimony.
You may feel you have no platform;
no theological training;
no special gift.
But you have one thing:
your story with the Lord.
And that often moves people most.
Because people can argue theology,
but they find it hard to deny a changed life.
Then in verse 19,
the Pharisees said:
"See how you accomplish nothing."
They had wanted to stop Jesus.
To suppress Him;
to destroy Him;
to keep people from following Him.
But the result was the opposite.
More and more people came;
the influence grew greater and greater;
Jesus' fame spread in every direction.
So they sighed:
"Behold, the world has gone after him."
Although these words carried complaint,
they unwittingly stated an important truth.
God's work
cannot be stopped by anyone.
The Pharisees thought they controlled the situation,
but in reality God was ruling history.
They wanted to shut the gospel down,
but the gospel spread ever wider.
They wanted to destroy Jesus,
but Jesus was going to save all peoples through the cross.
Later church history proved this again and again.
The Roman Empire persecuted Christians;
yet the gospel spread across the earth.
Many regimes tried to destroy the Bible;
yet the Bible became the most widely distributed book in the world.
Because:
human plans are limited,
but God's purpose endures forever.
This also gives us great comfort.
Today the world is full of turmoil;
faith faces challenges;
values change rapidly.
Sometimes we worry:
Will God's kingdom decline?
Will the gospel fail?
Will the church disappear?
The answer is no.
Because the church is not man's property,
but the body of Christ.
God's kingdom is not maintained by people,
but built by God Himself.
Jesus once said:
"I will build my assembly, and the gates of Hades will not prevail against it."
Therefore,
we need not be afraid.
We only need to be faithful.
This passage reminds us:
First, those who truly experience the Lord naturally bear witness. A life of grace cannot stay hidden long.
Second, God often uses people's testimonies to draw more people to know Jesus. Your story may become a blessing to someone else.
Third, people can oppose God but cannot stop God. God's purpose is always accomplished.
Fourth, the greatest power of the gospel comes from God Himself. It is not human ability but God's might.
Fifth, our responsibility is not to make God succeed but to follow Him faithfully. The outcome is in God's hands.
This passage also makes us think:
after Lazarus was raised,
the most natural result was testimony.
In the same way,
when a person truly experiences Christ,
his life will show change.
The 321 principles often remind us:
change the mindset and you change life;
change life and you change daily living;
change daily living and you change relationships;
change relationships and you change ministry.
A truly powerful testimony
is not saying how good we are,
but letting people see:
Jesus truly changed a person.
q: If others looked only at your daily life, could they tell that Jesus is at work in you?
Have you had a chance lately to share what God has done in your life?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You for doing wonderful work in our lives. Make us faithful witnesses, proclaiming You not only with our mouths but by living You out with our lives. When we face difficulty and challenge, let us also believe: Your kingdom can never be shaken, and Your purpose will surely be accomplished. May we follow You faithfully all our lives and glorify Your name. We pray in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, amen.

v: Now there were certain Greeks among those that went up to worship at the feast.
These, therefore, came to Philip, who was from Bethsaida of Galilee, and asked him, saying, “Sir, we want to see Jesus.”
Philip came and told Andrew, and in turn, Andrew came with Philip, and they told Jesus.
b: This passage seems ordinary,
yet it is a very important turning point in John's Gospel.
Because this is the first clear record of
Gentiles coming on their own to seek Jesus.
On the surface,
it is just a few Greeks wanting to see Jesus.
But from the viewpoint of God's history of salvation,
it symbolizes:
all nations and peoples beginning to turn to Christ.
God's promise to Abraham
is being fulfilled step by step.
The text says:
"Now there were certain Greeks."
The "Greeks" here
mostly means Gentiles influenced by Greek culture.
They may have been God-fearing Gentiles
who came to Jerusalem especially to worship at the feast.
Yet
in their hearts there was a deeper longing.
They did not only want to take part in religious activities;
did not only want to keep the festival;
did not only want to watch the crowd.
They wanted to see Jesus.
Many people today are the same.
Some come to church
at first because a friend invited them;
some because they have run into trouble in life;
some because they are looking for answers about life.
There are many surface reasons,
but at the deepest level there is really only one:
the human soul is seeking God.
As Augustine said:
"You made us for Yourself,
and our heart is restless
until it rests in You."
In the human heart there is an empty place,
that only God can fill.
Verse 21 records them saying:
"Sir, we want to see Jesus."
This is one of the most beautiful requests in John's Gospel.
Not:
we want to see a miracle;
not:
we want blessings;
not:
we want our problems solved;
but:
"We want to see Jesus."
These words are really the core of all spiritual seeking.
True faith
does not first pursue power;
does not first pursue gifts;
does not first pursue success;
but pursues Jesus Himself.
Many people seek God
when they are really seeking God's gifts.
But a mature faith
begins to seek the Lord who gives the gifts.
David once said:
"One thing I have asked of Yahweh, that I will seek after."
He was not seeking a throne;
not seeking victory;
but seeking God Himself.
Because only God
is the true satisfaction of life.
These Greeks had no idea
that their short sentence
would touch a moment in the whole history of salvation.
Because next Jesus will declare:
"The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified."
Why?
Because the Gentiles had begun to seek Him.
This meant:
the cross was about to come;
salvation was about to open to all peoples.
From then on,
God's kingdom would no longer be limited to the Jews,
but would open to the whole world.
Verse 22 mentions:
"Philip came and told Andrew."
Interesting,
neither disciple handled it directly.
They went together to see Jesus.
This shows us a beautiful spiritual principle:
when people seek Jesus,
our responsibility is not to bring them to ourselves,
but to the Lord.
Andrew has a particular trait in the Gospels.
He was always bringing people to Jesus.
He brought Peter to Jesus;
brought the boy with five loaves and two fish to Jesus;
and now helped bring the Greeks to Jesus.
Andrew may not have shone like Peter,
yet he was one who quietly brought people to the Lord.
Many times,
the most precious work in God's kingdom
is not standing on the stage shining,
but working behind the scenes to bring people to Jesus.
This is exactly the mission of a true disciple.
Not to make people depend on us;
not to make people worship us;
but to make people know Jesus.
This passage reminds us:
First, the deepest need of the human heart is actually God. Behind every search lies a longing of the soul.
Second, a mature faith seeks Jesus Himself. Not only seeking blessings, but seeking the Lord.
Third, God's salvation is prepared for all peoples. Jesus came not just for one nation but for the whole world.
Fourth, our responsibility is to bring people to Jesus. True ministry is leading people to know the Lord.
Fifth, God delights to use quiet, faithful people. Like Andrew, quietly be a bridge for others.
This passage also makes us reflect:
if someone today asked:
"I want to see Jesus."
then through our lives,
could he come closer to Jesus?
Or would he see only us?
A true disciple
does not make people stay on himself,
but lets people, through him,
see Christ.
q: What do you most long to receive from God right now? God's grace, or God Himself?
Are you becoming someone who brings people to Jesus?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, give us a heart that longs for You. Do not let us seek only blessings and grace, but long more deeply for Jesus Himself. Make us also a bridge, bringing people to the Lord. May our whole lives answer this beautiful longing: "Lord, we want to see You." We pray in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, amen.

v: Jesus answered them, “The time has come for the Son of Man to be glorified.
Most certainly I tell you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone. But if it dies, it bears much fruit.
He who loves his life will lose it. He who hates his life in this world will keep it to eternal life.
If anyone serves me, let him follow me. Where I am, there my servant will also be. If anyone serves me, the Father will honor him.
b: This passage is a very important turning point in John's Gospel.
Earlier the Greeks came seeking Jesus,
signifying that the Gentile world was beginning to open to Christ.
And Jesus immediately declared:
"The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified."
Surprisingly,
the glory Jesus spoke of
was not enthronement;
not coronation;
not the acclaim of all;
but the cross.
Man's glory is being lifted up;
God's glory is self-giving.
Man's glory is receiving;
God's glory is giving out.
Man's glory is being served;
God's glory is serving others.
Therefore,
Jesus redefined glory.
True glory
is not how much one has,
but how much one is willing to pay for love.
In verse 24,
Jesus used an extremely simple yet profound illustration:
"Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone."
People then all understood farming.
If a grain of wheat stays in the barn forever,
it will always be one grain.
Safe;
whole;
no loss.
But also no fruit.
Yet
if it is willing to be buried in the soil,
its shell broken,
seeming to be lost,
it can bring forth new life.
In the end it bears thirty, sixty, a hundredfold.
Jesus was first speaking of Himself.
He is that grain of wheat.
If He had not gone to the cross,
He would still be the one and only Son of God.
But through the cross and resurrection,
countless people received salvation
and became God's children.
Therefore,
the cross is not failure,
but the greatest harvest.
Yet
this principle applies not only to Jesus,
but to every disciple.
In God's kingdom there is an important law:
give first, then receive;
die first, then live;
humble first, then be lifted up.
The path of the grain of wheat
is also the path of the disciple.
In verse 25,
Jesus applied this principle to life.
He said:
"He who loves his life loses it."
The word "life" here
in the original also carries the sense of "self."
The meaning is:
making everything center on self;
protecting self;
exalting self;
insisting on self.
Such a person
ends up losing true life instead.
Because the more people hold on to themselves,
the narrower life becomes.
The more self-centered,
the less free.
This is exactly the root of human fall.
Adam and Eve wanted to rule themselves;
the people at Babel wanted to make a name for themselves;
people in every age have wanted to hold on to their own throne.
The result has been confusion and pain.
Then Jesus said:
"he who hates his life in this world will keep it to eternal life."
This does not tell people to despise themselves;
nor does it deny the value of life.
It means:
no longer being centered on self.
Being willing to hand the lordship of life to God.
Being willing to let Jesus be King.
This is the way of the cross.
It is also an important practice of the "self-denied" life in the 321 principles.
Not having no self,
but no longer letting self sit on the throne.
Not self as king,
but letting Jesus be King.
When people are willing to lay themselves down,
they gain true freedom instead.
When people are willing to lose,
they gain eternity instead.
In verse 26,
Jesus went further:
"If anyone serves me, let him follow me."
Many people want to serve the Lord
but do not want to follow the Lord.
They want power
but do not want to carry the cross.
They want the crown
but are unwilling to walk the way of the cross.
Yet
Jesus said:
serving and following cannot be separated.
True service
is not doing many things for the Lord;
it is living out the Lord's life.
As Jesus walked,
so we walk.
As Jesus gave up Himself,
so we learn to give up ourselves.
Then He promised:
"Where I am, there will my servant also be."
This is great grace.
We do not walk alone;
the Lord walks with us.
One day,
not only in this life will we walk with the Lord,
but in the future we will be with the Lord forever.
Finally Jesus said:
"if anyone serves me, the Father will honor him."
This is a stirring promise.
The Master of the universe
honors those who faithfully follow Him.
The world's applause will pass;
people's praise will vanish;
but the Heavenly Father's approval lasts forever.
A truly valuable life
is not to gain human glory,
but to gain God's pleasure.
This passage reminds us:
First, God's glory is often displayed through self-giving. The cross is not failure but the way of glory.
Second, the principle of the grain of wheat is a law of God's kingdom. Die first, then live; give first, then receive.
Third, the self-centered person ends up losing life. The Christ-centered person gains eternal life.
Fourth, true service must begin with following. Living out the Lord's life matters more than finishing the work.
Fifth, the Heavenly Father will honor those who faithfully follow Him. God's approval far surpasses human applause.
q: In what areas of your life are you still clinging tightly to yourself, unwilling to give to God?
Are you willing to be the grain of wheat that falls into the ground, so God can bear more fruit of life through you?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, help us understand the truth of the grain of wheat. Do not let us only want to protect ourselves, but be willing to place our lives in Your hands. Remove the pride and self-centeredness within us, and teach us to walk the path Jesus walked. May we become lives that bear fruit, glorifying You all our days and gaining Your pleasure. We pray in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, amen.

v: “Now my soul is troubled. What shall I say? ‘Father, save me from this time?’ But I came to this time for this cause.
Father, glorify your name!” Then a voice came out of the sky, saying, “I have both glorified it, and will glorify it again.”
Therefore the multitude who stood by and heard it said that it had thundered. Others said, “An angel has spoken to him.”
Jesus answered, “This voice hasn’t come for my sake, but for your sakes.
b: This passage shows us a most real side of Jesus.
He is not a God without feelings;
not a cold machine completing a mission;
He is the Son of God who truly became man.
Therefore,
as the cross drew nearer,
He also went through deep struggle.
At the beginning of verse 27,
Jesus said:
"Now my soul is troubled."
The original carries the sense of:
shaken;
grieved;
extremely disturbed.
This is one of the few places in John where Jesus' inner struggle is directly described.
Jesus knew what was about to happen.
He knew:
He would be betrayed;
humiliated;
scourged;
crucified;
and more importantly,
He would bear the sin of the whole world.
So,
His heart was extremely heavy.
This shows us:
faith does not mean having no emotions.
Jesus also grieved;
also was sad;
also suffered.
True spiritual maturity
is not pretending to have no feelings,
but still obeying God above those feelings.
Many Christians mistakenly think:
having sorrow means having no faith;
having tears means being spiritually poor.
That is not so.
Jesus Himself grieved.
The question is not whether we have emotions,
but whether our emotions lead us away from God.
Then Jesus said:
"What shall I say?"
This is a very real inner dialogue.
It is as if He were facing a choice.
Then He said:
"'Father, save me from this hour'?"
If we read only this sentence,
we might think Jesus wanted to avoid the cross.
But the next sentence at once reveals His heart:
"But for this cause I came to this hour."
This is the most important turning point in the whole passage.
Jesus did not deny the pain;
yet He chose to obey His mission.
It was not that He liked the cross;
but that He was willing to obey the Father.
This is the essence of true obedience.
If something costs nothing at all,
it is hard to call it obedience.
Obedience often happens when:
you want to quit yet choose to persevere;
you want to escape yet choose to face it;
you want to shrink back yet choose to go forward.
Jesus knew the pain of the cross,
yet still walked toward the cross.
Because He loved the Father,
and loved us.
Then He prayed:
"Father, glorify your name!"
This is the central aim of Jesus' life.
Not protecting Himself;
not fulfilling Himself;
not glorifying Himself.
But:
glorifying the Father.
This is also the portrait of Jesus' whole life.
From the manger in Bethlehem,
to ministry in Galilee,
to dying on the cross,
to resurrection and ascension,
everything He did
was to glorify the Father.
This is also the highest goal of a Christian's life.
Life is ultimately not about:
how much I get;
how successful I am;
how much I own.
It is about:
whether God is glorified through me.
Then,
the Heavenly Father responded in person:
"I have both glorified it, and will glorify it again."
This is a very important sentence in John's Gospel.
God the Father had already been glorified through Jesus' past ministry;
and next,
He would be glorified still more through the cross and resurrection.
In human eyes the cross is failure;
in God's eyes the cross is glory.
In human eyes suffering is shame;
in God's eyes obedience is glory.
This overturns the world's values.
Verse 29 says:
some heard the voice,
and said:
"It has thundered."
Others said:
"An angel has spoken to him."
The same voice,
yet different reactions.
This again shows:
the problem is often not whether God has spoken,
but whether people have heard.
God has always been working;
always guiding;
always speaking.
But if a person's heart is closed,
he hears only thunder.
In verse 30,
Jesus said:
"This voice hasn't come for my sake, but for your sakes."
The Father's testimony
was to strengthen people's faith.
Because God knew
that the coming cross would shake everyone.
He wanted the disciples to understand:
the cross is not failure;
but part of God's plan of salvation.
This passage reminds us:
First, Jesus also grieved. Faith is not the absence of emotion, but trusting God within the emotion.
Second, true obedience often comes with struggle. Obedience is not easy, but choosing God in the midst of difficulty.
Third, the greatest aim of Jesus' life was to glorify the Father. This should be the aim of our lives too.
Fourth, the cross looks like failure to people, but glory to God. God often accomplishes a greater purpose through suffering.
Fifth, God is always speaking. The problem is not God's silence, but whether we are willing to listen.
This passage also makes us think about the core of the 321 principles:
let Jesus receive all the glory.
When Jesus faced the cross,
He did not think of Himself first,
but said:
"Father, glorify your name."
When a person truly lives in this aim,
the direction of his life changes completely.
No longer centered on self,
but centered on God's glory.
This is the key to moving from a life with self to a life emptied of self.
q: When you face struggle, what comes first: your own interests, or God's glory?
If Jesus invited you today to walk the path of obedience with Him, would you?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, when we face difficulty and struggle, help us be like Jesus, not seeking only our own comfort and safety, but that Your will be done. Even when the road is hard, may we be willing to say: "Father, glorify Your name." May we not live for ourselves all our lives, but live for Your glory. We pray in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, amen.

v: Now is the judgment of this world. Now the prince of this world will be cast out.
And I, if I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself.”
But he said this, signifying by what kind of death he should die.
b: The twelfth chapter of John is leading us, step by step, toward the cross.
In human eyes,
the cross is failure;
is shame;
is death;
is the end.
But in God's eyes,
the cross is:
victory;
judgment;
salvation;
glory.
Therefore,
Jesus here unveils the true meaning of the cross.
At the beginning of verse 31,
Jesus said:
"Now is the judgment of this world."
Notice,
He did not say in the future,
but said:
"Now."
Because as Jesus walked toward the cross,
God had already begun to pass judgment on this fallen world's system.
The "world" here
is not just the earth,
but refers to:
values that oppose God;
a self-centered culture;
a system controlled by sin.
Since Adam sinned,
the world has fallen under the power of sin.
People make themselves king;
turn away from God;
pursue their own glory.
But the cross came,
and God began to judge all of this.
The cross is like a light
that shows people's true condition.
People think themselves good;
the cross reveals that people need salvation.
People think they can rely on themselves;
the cross reveals that people cannot save themselves.
Therefore,
the cross is first of all a judgment.
It reveals:
people cannot be saved by themselves.
Then Jesus said:
"Now the prince of this world will be cast out."
The prince of this world
is Satan.
Of course,
Satan is still active;
still tempting people;
still deceiving the world.
But the cross has already decided his final defeat.
Like a war
whose outcome has been decided,
though its full realization still takes time.
The cross is that decisive victory.
Colossians 2:15 says:
"Having stripped the principalities and the powers, he made a show of them openly, triumphing over them in it."
Satan's greatest weapons are:
sin;
accusation;
death.
But Jesus on the cross
has already paid the debt of sin;
removed the accusation;
overcome death.
Therefore,
Satan will surely be defeated in the end.
This is a great comfort to us.
Because many times,
we see the world dark;
see evil rampant;
see injustice.
It seems Satan is powerful.
But the cross tells us:
his end has been decided.
Christ has already won.
Then in verse 32,
Jesus gave a stirring promise:
"And I, if I am lifted up from the earth."
"Lifted up" in John's Gospel has a double meaning.
On one hand,
it refers to Jesus being nailed to the cross.
On the other hand,
it refers to His being glorified.
What the world saw was:
a crucified criminal.
What the Heavenly Father saw was:
the Lamb who had completed redemption.
The world saw shame;
God saw glory.
This is the most wonderful part of the gospel.
God takes what people consider the greatest failure
and turns it into the greatest victory.
Then Jesus said:
"will draw all people to myself."
Not by force;
not by control;
but by drawing.
The true gospel does not rely on threats.
The true gospel relies on love.
The greatest power of the cross
is not might,
but love.
When people see:
God was willing to die for me;
Christ was willing to bear the punishment in my place;
their hearts are drawn.
Countless people through the ages
have been drawn by the love of the cross.
Some scholars say:
no symbol in the world
has changed history like the cross.
Because the cross stands for:
sacrificial love;
forgiving love;
redeeming love;
love that never gives up.
Then Jesus said:
"draw all people to myself."
This is God's heart.
Salvation is not for a few;
but for all peoples.
From Genesis to Revelation,
God has been seeking the lost.
Whether:
Jew;
Gentile;
rich;
poor;
scholar;
fisherman;
man;
woman;
old;
child.
The cross is open to all.
Because God loved the world.
In verse 33,
John specially explains:
"But he said this, signifying by what kind of death he should die."
Jesus was not forced toward the cross.
He knew all along.
Step by step He walked toward Jerusalem,
step by step toward Golgotha,
step by step toward death.
Not because He was powerless to escape,
but because He willingly obeyed.
The cross is not a tragedy;
it is a choice of love.
This passage reminds us:
First, the cross is God's judgment on a sinful world. It shows that people cannot save themselves.
Second, the cross has already declared Satan's defeat. Christ is the conquering King.
Third, God often turns what people see as failure into glory. The cross is the best example.
Fourth, the greatest power of the cross is love. Christ draws people to Himself with love.
Fifth, salvation is open to all. God wants everyone to come to know Him.
This passage also makes us think:
what attracts people in the world today is:
money;
fame;
power;
pleasure.
But Jesus said:
what can truly draw people
is the love of the cross.
Because what the human heart most deeply needs
is not success,
but redemption.
Not applause,
but forgiveness.
Not the world,
but God.
q: To you, is the cross a religious symbol, or proof of God's love for you?
Are you willing to let Christ's love draw your heart again, to follow Him more deeply?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You for revealing, through the cross, how wide and long and high and deep Your love is. When we see Christ giving His life for us, draw us to You again. Help us also to live in Christ's victory, not held by darkness and fear. May we lift high the cross all our lives and proclaim salvation, so that more people are drawn by Your love. We pray in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, amen.
